paras.en: The Times investigation also found that Chavez had groomed and sexually abused girls as young as 12. Huerta said she had not been aware of Chavez’s sexual misconduct involving underage girls. “Unfortunately, he used some of his great leadership to abuse women and children—it’s really awful,” Huerta told Times.

In 2003, Huerta founded the Dolores Huerta Foundation, a social justice nonprofit, and promoted women candidates for public office as part of the Feminist Majority Foundation. She remained active into her later years, advocating for racial equality, economic justice, LGBTQ rights and women's rights.

Huerta earned numerous awards, including 15 honorary degrees and the Presidential Medal of Freedom. In 2019, California established an annual Dolores Huerta Day in recognition of her lifelong pursuit of justice.

“She made history,” Tey Marianna Nunn, associate director of content and interpretation at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Latino, tells Smithsonian magazine. “We can never forget the impact she has had on all of us.”

Huerta is credited with coining the phrase “Sí se puede,” or “yes we can,” which became a “rallying cry for workers, women, immigrants and people fighting for justice around the world,” according to the statement from her foundation. “She gave people the courage to recognize their own power—and showed them how to use it.”

articles.title: Paleontologists Discover the First Known Amphibian That Lived Entirely at Sea: a Flat, Armored Creature From 237 Million Years Ago

paras.en: Amphibians are known for straddling two worlds, dwelling on land and in water at different points in their lives. In fact, their name means “double life” in Greek. But no amphibian species has ever been known to reside exclusively in a marine environment—until now.

Two nearly complete fossilized skeletons found in southwestern China hint that an armored amphibian lived in the prehistoric salty waters there some 237 million years ago, researchers report in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution on October 26. The new species, named Gerrothorax maritimus, forces scientists to reconsider how today’s amphibians have adapted to their environments.

“This is potentially a revolutionary discovery,” says Steve Brusatte, a paleontologist at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland who wasn’t involved in the study, to Sarah Wild at Nature. “If this Triassic amphibian … really was fully marine, then it is a game-changer.” (The Triassic period stretched from 201 million to 252 million years ago.)

Out of the more than 8,000 amphibian species currently living on Earth, none are known to live in marine environments and only 2 percent have some level of salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. However, even this frog doesn’t do well in brackish water. That’s because amphibians have thin, permeable skin that allows them to breathe and consume water. When that skin is exposed to salt water, the animals become dehydrated.

“When a frog swims in sea water, it loses its body water because the sea water sucks out the body water through the permeable skin through osmotic pressure,” explains study co-author Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis, to Will Dunham at Reuters. “It cannot drink water either for the same reason. As a result, it loses body weight and will have to rest in freshwater to recover. This key feature prevents amphibians from becoming fully marine.”

So how could G. maritimus have accomplished a feat impossible for all amphibians today? The researchers suspect the answer lies in its unique biology and bony armor that would have prevented the animal from absorbing water through its skin. Instead, it had to drink water from its mouth, and its gills filtered out salt.
G. maritimus’ species name means “of the sea” in Latin.

G. maritimus was probably a flat, bottom-dwelling creature that sucked in prey that passed by. Multiple signs suggest the roughly 30-inch-long animal resided in the ocean. The fossils, unearthed in deep-sea sediments from Guizhou Province, China, were largely complete, suggesting the two amphibians died close to where they lived.

“Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” Motani explains in a statement. The species was also found next to an ancient marine reptile called an ichthyosaur. Moreover, Motani and colleagues measured the fossils’ proportions of different forms of the element strontium, a method used to date minerals and water. The proportions matched those of Late Triassic oceans, when the amphibian lived, the researchers found.

Anatomical analysis suggested that the closest relative of G. maritimus is G. pulcherrimus, an extinct amphibian that also lived during the Triassic. The two animals had similar armor and flattened bodies, although G. pulcherrimus lived in fresh water. That discovery led the researchers to conclude that G. maritimus’ marine lifestyle was an accident of evolution.
“There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonize the sea—the body armor,” Motani tells James Woodford at New Scientist.

Overall, the findings “reinforce the fact that the evolutionary and ecological relationships of amphibians with salt water are clearly much more complex and ancient than originally assumed,” says Gareth Hopkins, a zoologist at Western Oregon University who wasn’t involved in the study, to Nature. “At a time of rising sea levels and freshwater salinization, understanding how amphibians adapt and survive in salt water is critical to their conservation.”

articles.title: Drug-Resistant Germs Now Kill More Than 50,000 Americans Each Year, According to a New CDC Report

paras.en: Drug-resistant “superbugs” are now killing more than 50,000 Americans and infecting nearly 10 million each year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

This week, the federal health agency released its first comprehensive assessment of drug-resistant bacteria and fungi in seven years. The new report identifies 19 pathogens that currently pose a threat to human health in the United States, plus another six that are being monitored as potential threats.

Drug-resistant pathogens are those that have evolved to withstand the effects of medications designed to kill them or stop their growth, such as antibiotics, antifungals, antiparasitics and antivirals. Experts say the misuse and overuse of these treatments have contributed to the problem, along with environmental factors that seem to be helping superbugs thrive, like rising global temperatures.

When infections stop responding to standard treatments, patients may take longer to recover or end up with more severe illnesses. The risks are particularly high for people with compromised immune systems, underlying health conditions or those who use medical devices such as catheters and ventilators.

Patients in hospitals and other medical settings are also at increased risk. The CDC estimates that infections commonly associated with health care settings were responsible for more than 42,000 deaths and nearly $12 billion in health care costs in 2023.

Superbugs “prolong hospital stays, drive up health care costs and make it increasingly difficult—and sometimes impossible—for doctors to safely provide care,” Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America and an infectious-disease specialist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, says in a statement.
Did you know? A.I.-designed viruses could help with antimicrobial resistance

In August, researchers reported that they used artificial intelligence to design viruses not found in nature. The pathogens they made attack only bacteria, so the scientists propose that this technique could eventually help create treatments for antibiotic-resistant germs.

The new report classifies drug-resistant pathogens into three threat levels: urgent, serious or concerning. It also includes a watch list of potentially risky germs that researchers are still investigating to understand the threat they pose.

“The rankings are a way to differentiate the ones that we have the most lost sleep over at CDC,” says Michael Craig, who co-authored the new report and directs the CDC’s Antimicrobial Resistance Coordination and Strategy Unit, tells NBC News’ Aria Bendix. “But the thing that I always remind people is that all of these are threats.”

Four germs are listed as urgent, the highest level of threat. One is Candida auris, a fungus that spreads easily in hospitals and can cause illnesses ranging from mild skin infections to life-threatening bloodstream infections. According to the CDC, C. auris clinical cases increased by more than 50 percent between 2022 and 2023. And since 2019, the number of cases has increased nearly tenfold.

Another urgent superbug is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the bacterium that causes the sexually transmitted infection gonorrhea. It has become resistant to nearly every antibiotic used to treat it, and “it’s only a matter of time until it becomes resistant to the last available cure,” per the CDC.

The other two urgent germs are Acinetobacter and Enterobacterales, bacteria that commonly spread in health care settings. They are now resistant to even the most powerful antibiotics, including carbapenem antibiotics, so patients who develop infections have limited treatment options.

Overall, the report paints a troubling picture. But it also points to reasons for optimism. For example, the CDC has downgraded Clostridioides difficile, or “C. diff,” a bacterium that can cause diarrhea and colon inflammation. Cases are declining, dropping from 455,560 in 2018 to 412,504 in 2023, likely due to better diagnosis and infection prevention and treatment efforts.
The new report “shows both the progress we’ve made and the significant work that remains,” Erica Schwartz, director of the CDC, says in a statement.

The CDC last issued a report on drug-resistant bacteria and fungi in 2019. However, the agency cautioned against comparing numbers from the two assessments because it used different data sources and methods this time around. Moving forward, the CDC plans to release an update every two years, per NBC News.

Beyond the U.S., superbugs are a growing threat to public health around the world. Research suggests that antibiotic-resistant infections could result in more than 39 million deaths by 2050. Researchers are racing to develop new drugs that could help address the problem, but experts worry that these efforts may not keep pace with the growing threat.

“The scientific community has developed and approved new antibiotics in recent years,” said Yvan Hutin, previously the director of antimicrobial resistance at the World Health Organization, in a statement earlier this year. “This is good, but unfortunately not sufficient to catch up with evolving drug-resistant bacteria, especially against those of greatest concern. We need a reliable pipeline with new antibacterial agents that are innovative, affordable, accessible to all those who need them.”

articles.title: An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
articles.author: Emily Mullin

paras.en: If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.

Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.

Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.

“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.

AI models are trained primarily on published scientific literature. That means they may miss important information about the research process, including failed experiments, unexpected observations, and decisions scientists make in real time. Integrating AI models with real-world experiments can make the models more reliable, Santero says.

It’s why his team decided to connect an AI agent to a custom-built surgical setup used for performing brain injections on mice. The rig included a motorized device used to immobilize a mouse and a camera that allowed the agent to observe the procedure, move an injection needle, and control the delivery of a compound. For the experiment, his team was testing a gene therapy to see whether it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.

They asked the AI model to choose a treatment from 19 options in a spreadsheet. A veterinary surgeon first performed a craniotomy on the mouse while the AI agent observed. The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.

The team initially tested Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, but it refused to guide the needle into the mouse’s brain, suggesting it might stop midway through the surgery, which could endanger the animal.

“He did the experimental planning, but when it was time to inject, he said, ‘something on my output is telling me I shouldn't do this,’” Santero says, referring to the agent. “That was very interesting.”

The team switched to using Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Opus is a heavy-reasoning intelligence specialist best for complex multistep problem-solving, according to Anthropic, while Sonnet is better suited for everyday tasks, though it may be a stretch to call mouse brain surgery a common chore. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)

Frontier labs have been planning for more widespread physical manifestations of AI, and researchers have already begun enlisting agents to do other things in the physical world. In August, Anthropic put out a framework for how its models can interact with the real world. More recently, AI engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a car to pick up lunch at In-N-Out Burger. Only one of the models succeeded.

The brain injection procedure wasn’t without hiccups either. The researchers had established safeguards, including requiring the AI to propose an injection plan for human approval and installing an emergency button a human could hit that would disconnect the rig’s motors. They also restricted the agent's access to the underlying equipment code to prevent it from modifying its own operating rules.

However, a technical glitch disrupted the equipment's coordinate system. Although the agent correctly recognized that the calculated injection position was wrong, it refused to modify the code to correct the problem because its instructions explicitly prohibited doing so.

The team resolved the issue by using a separate AI agent on Opus 5 to make the necessary code changes, but they didn’t tell the agent that a live surgery was happening. The resulting back and forth delayed the procedure, Santero says: A typical brain injection surgery like this takes about 45 minutes, while this experiment lasted slightly longer than an hour. They’re now waiting for the therapy to take effect before assessing its impact on seizures.

Despite those glitches, Santero and his team were impressed by the agent’s performance. They’re testing Grok and other models next to figure out whether one model performs better. The company is also experimenting with agent-controlled craniotomies—a much more complicated task—but wants to be absolutely sure of their safety before moving to live surgeries.
“A mistake at that stage could seriously harm the mouse,” he says.

Santero thinks AI agents will increasingly work alongside human scientists, with direct access to lab equipment. For now, he says human oversight is key, particularly when experiments involve living animals. And it’s far too soon to unleash an AI agent on a human brain.
As for the mouse, Santero reports it’s recovering well.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
articles.author: Paresh Dave

paras.en: Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.

Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.

Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”

While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”

The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.

Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.
Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.

Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents.

Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said.

Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email.

There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement.

Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent. But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.

articles.title: Backup by Biolite Review: A Cool Idea
articles.author: Christopher Null

paras.en: Every part of a power outage is always a massive nuisance, but nothing is quite as aggravating as losing power to your refrigerator and the resultant spoilage of everything inside it.

Homes with a whole-house battery backup can avoid this headache, but the cost for a system like a Tesla Powerwall can easily hit $15,000 after installation. It takes an awful lot of melted ice cream for those numbers to balance out.

BioLite—known for its range of lighting and portable power solutions—is on the cusp of launching an alternative to whole-house batteries. Backup by BioLite is a modular battery system designed specifically with the fridge in mind, offering long-term emergency power at a fraction of the cost of more complex systems and which homeowners can install themselves. I installed it in my home and found it a capable (if limited) way to get a little extra peace of mind.

Backup by BioLite is hardly a difficult concept to grasp. The massive battery—offering 1526 watt-hours of power with a rated output of 1800 watts (and supporting peak surges up to 3000 watts)—mounts on the wall behind your refrigerator, or it can simply sit on top of it. The power pack measures 29 inches high by 13 inches wide, and a single unit weighs a hefty 40 pounds. No special wiring is required. You simply plug the Backup into a standard 120-volt outlet, then plug your refrigerator into the Backup.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Want more power? Backup’s Core unit can be daisy-chained to a Backup Extend add-on device, an identically sized (but slightly lighter) unit that doubles the power capacity to 3072 Wh.

Depending on your refrigerator, the full “Backup Complete” solution, with two cells, can provide up to 60 hours of running time if the grid goes down. If that’s not enough, additional Backup Extend devices can be added in series, with a total maximum capacity of 10.5 KWh. (Though, at that point, you may as well spring for a whole-house solution.)

One of the biggest selling points of Backup by BioLite is that you can install it yourself, with no electrician. I’ve got no trouble wielding a drill, so I undertook the effort to see if BioLite’s promise of a 30-minute install would pan out. I tested Backup Complete, with two Backup batteries situated side by side.

The process seems straightforward (and is enhanced by a helpful printed manual), but I quickly learned that my refrigerator’s location—tucked into an alcove—would complicate things because of the limited space in which to work. BioLite suggests having an extra pair of hands to hoist the heavy battery packs into place, but there was simply no room for my wife to squeeze into the alcove to help with any of the process. I managed on my own, but I expect this will present a challenge for some.

articles.title: California woman accused of deliberately running over 9-week-old puppy

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- A 75-year-old woman in California faces federal charges after allegedly luring a 9-week-old puppy beneath her minivan with food and running over the animal, killing it, prosecutors said Friday.
Hanh Minh Nguyen, of Anaheim, was charged Thursday with animal crushing, a federal felony punishable by up to seven years in prison.
Prosecutors said investigators obtained surveillance video showing a woman releasing a black-and-white pit bull puppy from a Honda Odyssey minivan in September.
The video allegedly shows the woman dropping food near the driver's door and gesturing for the puppy to approach.
As the vehicle moved forward, its rear tire ran over the animal.
Prosecutors said the driver stopped with the vehicle resting on the puppy for about 15 seconds before leaving.
An examination of the animal's remains found that it died from a crushed skull and suffered severe pain for several minutes before its death.
Police identified Nguyen as the suspected driver and arrested her Oct. 1.
She also faces animal cruelty charges in Orange County Superior Court.

articles.title: Former Army contractor charged with leaking military information

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- A former U.S. government contractor was arrested after allegedly sharing classified military information on social media and stealing night-vision equipment from an Army Special Operations facility, officials said Friday.
James Thomas Ashbacher, 37 of Spring Lake, N.C., was arrested Tuesday by the FBI following a federal indictment accusing him of unlawfully transmitting and keeping national defense information.
He also faces a charge of stealing government property.
Prosecutors said Ashbacher began working in 2021 for a private company that provided security and emergency management services at Fort Bragg.
His position gave him access to classified military information through a top-secret security clearance.
Investigators said Ashbacher photographed and copied material depicting classified military operations without authorization.
He allegedly uploaded the images and videos to a social media platform, where other users later shared them on another site.
A search of his home uncovered an award document containing classified defense information, investigators said.
Agents also recovered a night-vision system belonging to an Army Special Operations unit that had previously been reported missing.

articles.title: Calif. Botox doctor gets 15 years for $45 million Medicare fraud

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- A California doctor who fraudulently billed Medicare $45 million for Botox injections while she was vacationing in Mexico and other destinations was sentenced to 15 years in prison, officials said Friday.
Violetta Mailyan, 45 of Glendale, was sentenced Thursday for defrauding Medicare through her medical practice, Healthy Way Medical Center.
Prosecutors said Mailyan submitted more than $45 million in fraudulent claims for Botox treatments that were unnecessary, performed for cosmetic reasons or never administered.
Medicare covers Botox injections for certain medical conditions, including chronic migraines, but does not generally pay for cosmetic procedures.
Investigators found that Mailyan billed Medicare for thousands of treatments supposedly performed on days when her clinic was closed. Those claims totaled more than $19 million.
Prosecutors said she also submitted claims for treatments in California while traveling in Mexico, Hawaii, Las Vegas, Pennsylvania and New York.
During one trip to Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, Mailyan billed Medicare more than $200,000 for services she supposedly provided while away.
Mailyan attempted to conceal the fraud by creating false medical records and forging patient signatures after learning she was under investigation.
One of the patients she claimed to have treated was serving time in federal prison when the supposed appointment took place.
Prosecutors said Mailyan spent proceeds from the scheme on luxury purchases, including two Tesla vehicles, a Cybertruck and five properties in California.
Her purchases also included a 17th-century crossbow valued at $12,000 and a $3,000 painting.
A federal jury convicted Mailyan in May on nine counts of wire fraud and three counts of obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation.
The court ordered her to pay more than $32.9 million in restitution to Medicare.
She must also surrender more than $16 million in assets seized by federal authorities, including real estate, investments and bank funds.

articles.title: ‘SNL’ Parodies Nicki Minaj After Her Trump Rally Appearance
articles.author: Jessica Lynch

paras.en: Saturday Night Live turned its Halloween cold open on Saturday (Oct. 31) into a send-up of Nicki Minaj’s support for President Donald Trump, a week after the rapper joined him on the campaign trail.

Cast member Saidah Belo-Osagie played Minaj, bursting into the sketch near its end as James Austin Johnson’s Trump praised her loyalty to his movement. “Trump’s out here killing it,” Belo-Osagie’s Minaj declared, “and by it, I mean my career.” The sketch also cast her as Trump’s next choice for White House press secretary.

The parody drew directly on Minaj’s appearance at Trump’s Oct. 25 rally in Port Huron, Michigan, where she traveled with him on Air Force One and backed Republican candidates Mike Rogers and John James ahead of Tuesday’s (Nov. 3) midterm elections. During the rally, Trump invited Minaj to stand before the crowd and commented on her appearance, a moment the sketch played on with Johnson’s Trump making a string of jokes about the subject.

The press secretary gag also had a real-world source. A Trump staffer floated Minaj for the role during the Air Force One trip, and Trump later told The Benny Show it was “a good idea,” adding, “I’m gonna think about that.” Minaj has also said she is “not going anywhere” after Trump called her his “favorite.”

The cold open was framed as a ride through a budget Halloween haunted attraction, with Grace Reiter and Jeremy Culhane as a couple on a date and Kenan Thompson as a Grim Reaper guide. Tom Hanks then appeared as David S. Pumpkins, the oddball character he introduced on the show in 2016, backed by his dancing skeleton sidekicks Mikey Day and former cast member Bobby Moynihan, in what the sketch itself called the character’s third outing.

Before the bit could get going, Johnson’s Trump froze the scene and cut it short. “I’ll save you four minutes: he keeps popping up and confusing people on the ride. The end,” he told the audience, before comparing himself to Pumpkins: “We both appeared in 2016, we’re both very loud, very orange.” He went on to complain about Republican polling ahead of the midterms before Belo-Osagie’s Minaj made her entrance.
Minaj has not publicly addressed the sketch.

The rapper remains one of the most successful acts in Billboard chart history. In 2018, she became the first woman to log 100 entries on the Billboard Hot 100, and she holds the most Hot 100 top 10s among female rappers. In 2020, she and Doja Cat became the first female rap duo to top the Hot 100, with the remix of “Say So.”

Obsession star Inde Navarrette hosted the episode, her first time in the role. Gracie Abrams was the musical guest, her second SNL appearance after her December 2024 debut. She arrived fresh off the release of her new single “Here You Come, There You Go” on Oct. 29, and ahead of her Look at My Life arena tour, which launches Dec. 2 in Denver in support of her third album, Daughter From Hell.
SNL airs live on Saturday (Oct. 31), with a start time of 11:30 p.m. ET/PT.

articles.title: Tovah Feldshuh Shuts Down ‘Nobody Wants This’ Cast Tension Rumors Amid Adam Brody “Free Palestine” Support
articles.author: McKinley Franklin

paras.en: Nobody Wants This actress Tovah Feldshuh is shutting down claims that tensions are rising among the cast amid recent comments Adam Brody made saying he is in support of “a free Palestine.”

“Tensions are NOT RISING. Profound differences of opinion are. Please do not conflate the two — And none of it will be brought to the set,” she wrote in response to a Threads post made by AzatTV that reads, “Tensions are emerging on the set of the Netflix series Nobody Wants This.”
Feldshuh added, “I deeply enjoy filming [Nobody Wants This] and hope we are chosen to go on for a fourth season.”

In an interview with GQ, Brody said of the war in Gaza, “put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.” He added, “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”

Feldshuh, who plays the mother of Brody’s character Noah on the Netflix show, told The New York Post of the actor’s comments, “To accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild.” She added, “It’s right out of Hitler’s playbook. You take the victim and you make the victim the perpetrator.”
The actress said that it “makes a difference to the [Jewish] community,” when asked by the Post if “accusations of genocide are worse when they come from Jewish people themselves.”

“I believe that the perseverance of the existence of the state of Israel is crucial to the well-being of the democratic world and of the free world,” Feldshuh said. “Of course, Israel needs the United States, [but] the United States needs Israel, believe you me.”
Feldshuh also told the outlet, “My job, as Bina but also as Tovah, is to love the people on set at my place of work, to be kind.”
She added, “With the backdrop of global antisemitism, I am thrilled to be chosen to play a Jewish matriarch. Thrilled and proud, and that will never change.”
Erin Foster, creator of Nobody Wants This, has also reacted to Brody’s statement, saying on the Not Skinny But Not Fat podcast that “it’s complicated.”

“I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing,” Foster said. “While I love Adam, I also disagree with him, and that’s okay.”

“I think that as the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel,” she continued. “And the show has always been and always will be a love letter to Judaism. That is why I made this show. It’s because of how beautiful of an experience I’ve had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person, and sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people, I think it’s so important to have that.”

articles.title: Heidi Klum Reveals This Year’s (Very Bloody) Halloween Costume
articles.author: Kirsten Chuba

paras.en: It wouldn’t be Halloween without Heidi Klum, as the star revealed yet another jaw-dropping costume at her signature party on Saturday night.
The Queen of Halloween, as she has become known, celebrated the 25th anniversary of her NYC Halloween party this year, and Klum took it to the next level as she showed up as a severed hand.

She arrived in a truck covered in red “danger” sings, helped to the ground by actors in yellow hazmat suits. Klum’s elaborate costume includes a bloody wrist and her head at the center of the hand, with fingers featuring rings and a fresh manicure; she revealed in red carpet interviews it was an intricate recreation of her own hand. The star appeared without husband Tom Kaulitz, who has dressed up alongside her in recent years.

Klum is hosting the event, presented by Apothic and Butterfinger, at Cathédrale Restaurant at Moxy East Village. The party has become one of Spooky Season’s most iconic events, as Klum always turns up in an elaborate look — in recent years, she’s transformed into Medusa, E.T., a peacock, Fiona from Shrek, Jessica Rabbit and famously, a worm.

The supermodel has been teasing glimpses at her costume on her Instagram, teasing her transformation all day long while asking her followers to submit their guesses on what she would become. Klum collaborates on her costumes with special effects makeup designer Mike Marino, who won an Emmy for his work on The Penguin. Marino revealed in a recent interview that “this costume this year is one of the most elaborate costumes ever made. It’s so difficult to do and just the complication of it is really challenging.”

articles.title: ‘SNL’: Inde Navarrette Digs at Shane Gillis’ Joke About Women Dressing Like “Whores” at the Gym as Tom Hanks Crashes Cold Open
articles.author: McKinley Franklin

paras.en: Inde Navarrette made her Saturday Night Live hosting debut on the show’s Halloween episode, and kicked things off with a dig at the most recent host of the late night series.

The actress began her monologue by referencing her star-making role in Obsession: “You probably know me from the movie Obsession. People ask me if I’m anything like my character Nikki, and I’m like, no. No, no, don’t do that.”

“But the thing is, I’m nothing like my character in Obsession. Like, my boyfriend is here tonight to support me,” she said, as the camera panned over to her boyfriend, Nick Aiello, duck-taped in the audience. “We have such a chill relationship, right?”

Navarrette went on to discuss how she’ll be next portraying Rogue in Marvel Studios’ X-Men reboot. The character preps requires a lot of working out, she noted. “I can’t believe I’m saying this, but I’m gonna be in a Marvel movie. I know it’s really important for Marvel that you get really fit, so I’ve been working out a lot.”
“So every morning, I put on my little whore outfit, and I hit the gym,” she said, in a callback to Shane Gillis’ controversial monologue on the most recent episode of SNL on Oct. 10.

During his SNL appearance, he said at the top of the episode, “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now. Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial vape-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look!”

Continuing with her monologue, Navarrette invited the SNL cast to the stage to show off their Halloween costumes “since none of the cast could go out tonight.” Marcello Hernandez appeared as “a sexy TSA agent,” as Kam Patterson portrayed Elizabeth Holmes.
Jeremy Culhane also joined, using his time during Navarrette’s monologue as an audition for Jake Schreier’s upcoming X-Men movie.

“I know you were cast as Rogue in the new X-Men movie, and I randomly heard they, like, I guess they haven’t even cast Wolverine yet,” Culhane said, to which Navarrette replied, “Oh, I’m so sorry. I can’t comment on that.”

“Well, I can, and I’d love to be in the movie with you,” Culhane, dressed as Wolverine, said. Grace Reiter then joined dressed up as none other than the bird at the center of the viral Kelly Clarkson, Art of Play controversy.
“It’s actually a group costume,” Reiter said, as Veronika Slowikowska popped in dressed like American Idol winner. “I want to buy the bird,” she said. “Sell me the damn bird!”
“I am not for sale!” Reiter as the bird said.
Tom Hanks’ classic Halloween character David S. Pumpkins made a surprise appearance in the cold open, opened by Reiter and Culhane as they embarked on a spooky ride.
James Austin Johnson’s Trump, of course, crashed the party to discuss the upcoming midterms.

“Are you sad you don’t get to see your third David Pumpkins scene? I’ll send you four minutes. He keeps popping up and confusing the people on the ride. ‘But you don’t actually have a lot in common with Mr. Pumpkins.’ We both appeared in 2016. We’re both very loud, very orange, and very frankly annoying,” Johnson’s Trump said.
“Good acting, great ass. A great ass on Hanks — something that I’ve enjoyed lately admiring,” he added. “Not that there’s anything wrong with that. Just that I might be gay.”

He was joined by Nicki Minaj (“my friend and future press secretary”), portrayed by Saidah Belo-Osagie, who showed her support for the president. “Trump’s out here killing it — and by it, I mean my career,” Belo-Osagie said.

“I’m Nicki, the Trumpy. Like, I don’t even know why you Democrats bother at this point. Like, give it up. It’s me,” she added before exiting the stage. “Thank you, Nicki. She’s got quite an ass. If only it were on a man, perhaps then I could admire it,” Johnson’s Trump said.
And Slowikowska also appeared as Katie Zacharia, Trump’s brief, former White House Press Secretary, to butcher SNL’s opening catchphrase, “Live from New York, it’s Saturday Night!”
She instead said, “With confidence. Live from New York. And from so many cities,” before she was cut off.

Pumpkins wasn’t the only character of SNL‘s past to pop up, as Bobby Moynihan’s Drunk Uncle appeared during the Weekend Update segment. He was even joined by the Milwaukee Brewers, the 2026 World Series champions. Christian Yelich, Brice Turang and team manager Pat Murphy were on hand to rep for the winning team. Moynihan even joked that Yelich was Pete Davidson.

Navarrette rose to acclaim this summer for her starring turn in Curry Barker’s new horror hit. She plays Nikki Freeman, a woman who is cursed after Bear (Michael Johnston) wishes that she’d love him more than anyone else in the world.

The low-budget film grossed over $522 million worldwide, breaking a plethora of records along the way: Obsession is Focus Features‘ biggest movie of all time; is the top-grossing festival acquisition (hailing from TIFF); and earned the biggest second-weekend box office spike in modern times outside of the Christmas holiday.
She’ll next star in Marvel Studios’ X-Men reboot, Apple Original Films’ sci-fi thriller The Waffle House Index, which she will also executive produce.
Saturday night marked Navarrette’s SNL debut, and she was joined by Gracie Abrams as musical guest. Elsewhere on season 52, Jalen Brunson, Dakota Johnson and Gillis have hosted.
After the Obsession actress, Druski will host on Nov. 7; he is the first social media influencer to ever host SNL. The Strokes will be the musical guest.
John Mulaney will host the Nov. 14 episode, and he’ll be joined by Phoebe Bridgers.
Before Saturday night’s episode, SNL shared a tribute for Patrick Stewart, featuring a clip from his 1994 appearance on the show.

articles.title: SpaceX loses bid to toss NAACP lawsuit over Memphis data center air pollution

paras.en: SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday.

The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis.
The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years.
The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026.

The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby."
(SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.)
The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit.

Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional.

The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed."
The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: OPEC+ agrees in principle to keep oil output targets steady in December, sources say

paras.en: OPEC+ oil-producing countries have agreed in principle to keep their December oil output targets steady at a meeting on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments won't occur until next year.

Sunday's online meeting of seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — comes as Gulf members have been boosting exports disrupted for months by the war with Iran. Most, however, are still pumping well below their output targets.
All three people declined to be identified.
OPEC+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies, including Russia.

In September, OPEC+ completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. Disruption caused by the Iran war has meant Gulf producers are falling below their quotas.
Reuters reported in July that OPEC+ was likely to make no changes to its targets during the fourth quarter as it turns its focus to 2027 quota negotiations.
The group still has one more layer of production cuts of about 2 million bpd covering most members through the end of 2026.

OPEC+ needs to finalize a review of members' production capacity during the fourth quarter before setting the 2027 baselines that will determine future quotas and shape plans to unwind those cuts, sources have said.
On Friday, oil prices surged more than 2%, settling at their highest levels since the end of April as traders braced for a potential escalation in the war.
Brent crude futures for December, which expired on Friday, closed up $2.76, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, after touching a high of $118. The more active January contract gained $2.63 to $113.43.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures ended $2.12, or 2.08%, higher at $104.12.

articles.title: Trump defamation suit against Murdoch, WSJ over Epstein letter dismissed with prejudice

paras.en: A federal judge in Miami on Saturday dismissed with prejudice President Donald Trump's amended defamation lawsuit against media baron Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal over the newspaper's reporting on a purported 50th birthday letter from the president to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
District Court Judge Darrin Gayles ruled that Trump had again failed to plausibly allege the newspaper and other defendants acted with actual malice when they published the story in July 2025.

"As with his first attempt, he has failed," Gayles wrote in the 20-page ruling, which came more than six months after he dismissed Trump's first version of the suit. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation."
By dismissing the suit with prejudice, the judge blocked Trump from filing another suit alleging the same claims about Murdoch and the paper in federal court.

Gayles said the Journal had conducted a "thoughtful and detailed investigation," and he rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should not have published the story after he denied writing the letter.
The judge did not determine whether Trump actually authored the disputed letter. Trump has adamantly denied writing it.
When Galyes first dismissed the suit in April, he allowed Trump to file an amended version of the complaint to cure legal defects the judge had identified.
Trump was seeking $10 billion in damages from Murdoch and the Journal, which is owned by Murdoch's News Corp.
A spokesperson for the newspaper's publisher, Dow Jones & Co., in a statement to CNBC on Saturday, said, "We're pleased with the court's decision."
A spokesman for Trump's legal team confirmed to CNBC that the president plans to appeal the ruling.

"President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants," the spokesman said in a statement. "The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions."

Gayles, as he did when dismissing the suit for the first time, noted Trump, who has adamantly denied sending the letter to his then-friend Epstein in 2003, had "not plausibly alleged that the Defendants published the Article with actual malice."

Plaintiffs who are public figures like Trump must show a defendant acted with actual malice when making allegedly defamatory statements, according to Supreme Court decisions that Gayles cited at the beginning of his ruling.

Trump's amended lawsuit contained new details and claims, including that Murdoch told the president "I will handle it" during a phone conversation they had about an article describing a birthday letter to Epstein that allegedly bore Trump's signature, Newsweek previously reported.

Gayles rejected each of Trump's arguments in the amended complaint, including that the Journal did not adequately investigate the letter, omitted relevant details, and that the article was published after the president and his representatives denied it was authentic.

Gayles said that accepting that last argument would effectively allow public figures to block unfavorable reporting, which "runs afoul of the First Amendment" that protects freedom of speech and the press.
Saturday's ruling is the latest setback in litigation between Trump and the media.
Another federal judge in Miami on Oct. 22 ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.
The Journal's article on July 17, 2025, said a letter bearing Trump's signature was included in an album of letters Epstein was giving for his 50th birthday.
The article said Trump sent the letter at the request of Epstein's close friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, who two decades later was convicted of procuring underage girls to be sexually abused by Epstein.
The Journal noted that the letter "contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker."

"A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly 'Donald' below her waist, mimicking pubic hair," Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo said in the article.
"The letter concludes: 'Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,'" they wrote.
Trump angrily denied writing the letter, saying, "This is not me. This is a fake thing."'
"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," the president said at the time.

articles.title: Scientists can now rewire living brains

paras.en: The human brain holds around 86 billion neurons, wired together in a vast web of hundreds of trillions of connections. These connections, bridged by structures called synapses, form circuits responsible for everything we feel, perceive and do. And they constantly shift as we grow, learn, make memories and form habits.

Neuroscientists have long sought to hack into these circuits to understand how the brain works. Just 20 years ago they developed a technique called optogenetics, which offered some of the first glimpses of these circuits in action—it uses light to turn cells, including brain cells, on and off.

The work won three scientists the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. If brain pathways were highways, optogenetics would be akin to “controlling the volume of traffic on a road network that’s already built,” says Sangkyu Lee, a neurobiologist at the Institute for Basic Science in South Korea.

Better yet, however, would be “changing the structure of the ‘road’ itself,” Lee says—by actually editing the brain’s connections. More recently, scientists have figured out how to add new connections and delete existing ones, and they have used these techniques to change animals’ behavior and even to implant memories. Ultimately, these tools could yield discoveries about the brain and potentially even treatments for psychiatric conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

paras.en: “The idea that, by manipulating brain activity, you could, in principle, make someone happy or sad, or thirsty or hungry, is incredible when you think about the ramifications,” says Don Arnold, a neurobiologist at the University of Southern California.

Kafui Dzirasa, a psychiatrist at Duke University, stumbled into “synaptic engineering” by accident. He had been trying to develop treatments for psychiatric conditions using brain-machine interfaces to alter neural activity. Electrodes would pick up activity in one brain region and cause a computer to stimulate another—essentially “wiring” the two regions together. But as a potential treatment for mental illness, it was impractical. So Dzirasa began contemplating other ways to connect two disparate brain regions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “We realized that’s what a synapse does, so we thought, ‘Why don't we just create a synapse?’” he says.

Neurobiologists had already developed a way to do this in a creature with a very simple brain: the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. It has only around 300 neurons, making it ideal for neuroscientists to study. In 2014 Ithai Rabinowitch, a neurobiologist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and his colleagues successfully altered the worms’ behavior by rewiring their neural circuits.

The team did this by creating a kind of synapse that passes electrically charged particles between two cells through special protein channels. These proteins are made by genes that are snuck into cells’ DNA using a specially programmed virus. Rabinowitch’s team inserted mouse synapse proteins into the worms, which created artificial connections that didn’t interfere with worms’ existing synapses. The researchers were able to alter a circuit governing the worms’ sense of smell, causing them to avoid an odor they previously found attractive.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This technique has since been used to study neural circuits involved in everything from defecation to learning. In one striking example, another team of researchers used it to rewire a memory. First, they trained worms to prefer a specific temperature. Then they bypassed the memory with an electrical synapse, causing the worms to move toward warmer temperatures instead. “It’s like an inception experiment, where you plant a memory by making an artificial connection,” says that study’s senior author Daniel Colón-Ramos, a cell biologist at the Yale School of Medicine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But could this approach work in the more complex brains of mammals? As brains get bigger and more complicated, the potential for unintended connections is harder to prevent—these can wreak havoc, potentially causing death. “You need to achieve much more control and precision in an animal with billions of neurons,” Colón-Ramos says.

In a study published in May, Dzirasa, Colón-Ramos and their team proved the technique could be done in a mouse. They created synapse proteins that only connected to a specially engineered partner—not to each other or to synapse proteins that were already in the mouse’s brain. They used the tool to connect different cell types in two brain circuits, producing changes in the mice’s behavior.

Some of these behavioral changes offer hints at parallels in human brains. In a study posted to the preprint server bioRxiv last March, Dzirasa and his colleagues tested the tool in mice with a genetic mutation that caused repetitive grooming behaviors reminiscent of OCD. The researchers introduced synapses to bypass the disrupted circuit, which reduced this pathological behavior. “That’s a clear demonstration of the potential power of this in thinking about human diseases,” Dzirasa says.

Researchers have developed other techniques for engineering new connections, too. But some situations may call for the opposite approach: deleting existing connections. For instance, PTSD can cause otherwise innocuous sights or sounds to trigger anxiety. These reactions may stem from connections formed between sensory neurons and “negative emotion” cells in the amygdala.
“It’s tantalizing to think, if you could wipe those synapses out, maybe you’d get rid of this,” Arnold says.

So far, synapse-deleting tools are much less precise than synapse-adding ones. For example, Arnold and his colleagues discovered a technique that degrades proteins that hold synapses together, deleting them from neurons en masse. Last year they expanded this into a toolkit that can delete only inhibitory or only excitatory synapses (which respectively make neurons less or more likely to fire) and that can be activated with light or chemicals.

And in a study in April, Lee and his colleagues described a slightly more precise synapse-deleting tool called Synthetic Trogocytosis, or SynTrogo, which works by recruiting astrocytes, a type of brain cell that prunes synapses naturally. Using special “lock” and “key” proteins to trigger pruning, Lee’s team was able to delete less than a third of specific cell types’ synapses in two parts of mice’s hippocampus, a brain region that is crucial for memory. The remaining connections became stronger, and the mice showed better performance than unedited animals in memory tests. This finding hints at potential applications in neurodevelopmental conditions that involve abnormal connectivity, such as schizophrenia, but also those involving memory impairment, such as dementia.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Having techniques that can delete as well as add synapses “gives much more versatility,” Colón-Ramos says. “You have a gas pedal, but now you also have brakes, so you can do much more.”

Looking ahead, Rabinowitch envisages a day when scientists can construct designer connectomes—entire brains’ worth of custom connections. “You sit by your computer and say, ‘Let’s build this brain,’” he says. “Then it spills out the list of genes you need to introduce into the organism, and you build your synthetic connectome.” Ultimately, this could produce edited animals that perform specific tasks or even artificial life, Rabinowitch says.
We are a long way from these techniques being used in humans. Optogenetics, the 20-year-old, Nobel Prize–winning technology, has only just proven itself safe in trials of human treatments.

To edit human circuits, researchers will have to figure out how to safely deliver DNA across the blood-brain barrier and into neurons. Scientists are working on brain delivery systems, but “that’s a barrier nobody’s really solved yet,” Arnold says. And no one knows how safe these new tools are. “We’re starting to test if human tissue can tolerate them,” Dzirasa says.

And perhaps more critically, researchers need to understand human brain function better before they can usefully intervene. Synaptic engineering may be just what’s needed to figure this out, however. “If you don’t know how something works, you cannot fix it,” Colón-Ramos says. “These tools will lead to the knowledge we need for any aspiration of healing.”

articles.title: Oldest known Mars rock is a ‘Rosetta stone’ for the Red Planet’s watery past

paras.en: In 2022 a group of nomadic meteorite hunters discovered a strange stone in the Sahara Desert. Called Teghaza 001, initial analysis by experts showed it was a meteorite from Mars. Now new research reveals it’s the oldest ever found, and it’s revealing more about the Red Planet’s complex history.

Scientists fortunate enough to get their hands on samples of the space rock have been analyzing tiny pieces of Teghaza for years to better understand exactly what it is and when it formed. The new paper, published today in Science, identifies it as a piece of Mars’s crust that’s at least 4.1 billion years old, from a time when that world was warmer, wetter and more Earth-like.

“We’re holding a piece of a rock that’s dated even before the oldest Earth rock—a piece of Mars that’s so ancient, it existed when life had just started on Earth,” says Yang Liu, lead author of the study and a planetary scientist at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Several hundred Martian meteorites are known. All of them got here by giant impacts that have pelted Mars for eons, occasionally blasting bits of the planet into space, some of which by chance fall to Earth. Most are relatively young, each revealing little more than a snapshot from the most recent 600 million years or so of Mars’s 4.5-billion-year history. The only other known intact ancient sample, a meteorite discovered in Antarctica in the 1980s, is just 10 million years younger than Teghaza.

When Liu received a piece of the rock from the team at the University of New Mexico that initially analyzed it, she was tasked with studying its manganese, an element that can help scientists discern whether an ancient rock was ever exposed to water and oxidation. But soon she noticed the presence of zircons in the meteorite—tough crystalline minerals that can endure in rock for billions of years and contain radioactive isotopes that can be used for ultraprecise dating. The zircons, Liu realized, made Teghaza very special. In the exhaustive work that followed, she and her team isolated zircons and other minerals from small scraps of their precious samples, pinning down the meteorite’s chemical composition and dating its elements to the early days of Mars’s history.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Teghaza, they found, is an igneous rock that formed from slowly-cooled magma and was once a piece of the planet’s crust. Comparing ratios of certain elements in the meteorite to those measured by orbiters for larger swaths of the planet’s surface, Liu and her team found the closest matches within the rugged, crater-pocked terrain in Mars’s southern highlands, a region thought to be among the world’s most ancient.

Pinpointing the possible sites where Teghaza was launched by a giant impact on its fateful journey to Earth is a feat all its own, but the meteorite’s chemical composition shows something even more enlightening.

As detailed in work from Liu’s team published earlier this year, some of the minerals in the meteorite have been aqueously altered—a sign that liquid water once percolated through Mars’s ancient mantle and crust. And careful analysis of remnant hydrogen trapped inside Teghaza shows that even when the rock formed, more than 4.1 billion years ago, the planet was already well on its way to losing most of its atmosphere, growing cold and transitioning to its current freeze-dried state. Taken together with the results in today’s paper, Liu says, all this reinforces how Mars’s mantle is likely more heterogeneous and complex than many planetary scientists have long assumed.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Liu’s research on Teghaza is ongoing; her team “has only scratched the surface,” she says, of the insights the meteorite might hold.

A clearer understanding of Mars’s deep past can also inform our own. Mars and Earth formed in similar ways, with giant magma oceans that cooled into cores, mantles and crusts. Because of its tectonic activity that continuously buries, melts and recycles the planet’s crust across geological time, Earth’s surface does not preserve many (if any) samples from its primordial youth—but Mars is different, as its geophysical tumults ebbed long ago.
One reviewer of the paper called this meteorite “the Rosetta stone of Mars,” Liu says, because it may be able to tell the stories of planets across the solar system.
“We’re hoping to start using Mars to compare and contrast and to understand what makes a planet habitable for life,” she adds.

There’s much still to learn about this meteorite’s mysteries, says Arya Udry, a planetary scientist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, who was not involved with the Science study. But truly understanding the full story of Mars requires more than gathering additional impact-imported fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth; what’s necessary is more visits to the world itself.
“Mars is a complex planet, and this meteorite is really cool, but we don’t know exactly where it came from, so this is really another example of why we need to bring back samples,” she says.

articles.title: The science of why we’re obsessed with vampires

paras.en: Rachel Feltman: Happy Halloween, listeners. For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.

When I was about 13 years old, I stumbled upon a vampire story that I became obsessed with. I wrote reams of fan fiction and made my crush on all three members of the main love triangle into an entire personality. Many girls on the cusp of teenhood in 2005 could no doubt say the same, though most of them were probably fixated on the recently released book Twilight, and I, ever the contrarian, had gone to my local Blockbuster and discovered a movie from 1987.
[CLIP: Kiefer Sutherland as David in The Lost Boys. “Now you know what we are. Now you know what you are. You’ll never grow old, Michael, and you’ll never die. But you must feed.”]

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

It’s been more than 20 years, but I’m still firmly Team Kiefer. So you can imagine my delight when, just this past April, a musical based on The Lost Boys made its Broadway debut. And that’s far from the only vampire media people are paying to see in droves: With his award-winning movie Sinners, Ryan Coogler brought creatures of the night into prestige cinema like never before. And AMC’s adaptation of Anne Rice’s The Vampire Chronicles series has launched her beloved character Lestat into the stratosphere.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: [CLIP: Sam Reid as Lestat in Interview with a Vampire: “Are there any readers in the audience tonight?”]

Then, of course there’s Robert Eggers’s Nosferatu, Cynthia Erivo’s solo Dracula show on the West End, the delightful comedy What We Do in the Shadows, which sadly has ended, Dimension 20’s “City Council of Darkness”—I could go on.

So today we’re going to talk about what makes vampires so fascinating that they keep showing up in our media—and how these seductive fictional figures can actually be traced back to public health horror stories.

Tales of humanoid creatures that feed on life are about as old as stories get, but the use of the term “vampire” for a bloodsucking monster seems to have emerged around 18th-century Europe. And throughout the [1700s] and 1800s, many people saw vampires as a real and present danger.
Aaron Mahnke: It’s just a bizarre story, you know. And there’s some grief involved in it, there’s some tragedy and some weirdness and some grossness, but at the core of it, it’s a fascinating story.
Feltman: That’s Aaron Mahnke, a historian who hosts the hit podcast Lore. His latest book is called Exhumed: Unearthing the History of the American Vampire.
Mahnke: What we think was going on was essentially a community would experience an outbreak, usually of what we think was tuberculosis because of the symptoms.

Feltman: Basically, people got it into their heads that certain illnesses could be transmitted posthumously, with the dead somehow staying tethered to the living and draining their health away. Because tuberculosis could spread between family members and then slowly kill several of them in a row, the disease might seem almost like a curse. Inventing vampires as an explanation helped people feel like there was something they could do to keep tragedies from multiplying.

Similar “epidemics” show up in earlier historical records around the world and were particularly common in Europe in the 1700s. But Mahnke’s book focuses on the story of Mercy Brown, who died of what was likely tuberculosis in Exeter, Rhode Island, in 1892.

Mahnke: You have to imagine these are people in the early to mid-1800s who had no concept of virology and how illness was passed around. So what people were doing was reacting to this belief that the reason why people in their family were sick was because someone who had already died from the sickness in their family was literally lying in their grave, drinking the life force from those who were still above ground. So not in a sense—like the vampire that we think of today as running around in leather pants with handguns and, you know, battling werewolves and drinking the blood out of someone’s neck. So in the century of the New England vampire panic, it was more Colin, the emotional vampire from What We Do in the Shadows. They were sucking the life from someone from a distance.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: You can see the threads that would eventually weave into the bloody vampire myths we know today in the methods New Englanders used to “prove” a vampire’s existence. Mahnke says folks had a pretty binary understanding of decomposition and the degradation of blood in particular. If a body was really and truly dead, they figured, blood would be dried into powder. The presence of liquid meant something was still kicking around in there. But there are a few reasons someone might see what seemed to be fresh blood in a definitely actually dead corpse: Liquids produced by decomposition might ooze out of orifices tinted red by dried blood, for one thing. And in New England and much of Europe, where death during winter meant loved ones were temporarily interred aboveground to wait for the ground to thaw, blood and tissue might freeze instead of rotting.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Mercy Brown, for instance, died in January and was “exhumed” that March.

Mahnke: Her exhumation was literally just opening a shed and removing her coffin. They miraculously discovered that she looked very well preserved, but that’s kind of what you’d expect from somebody who’d spent two months in a walk-in freezer.

Feltman: As Mahnke’s latest book makes clear, this visceral fear of the undead was really quite recent. Mercy Brown’s sister lived until 1954. But during her lifetime, our attitude toward vampires made a radical shift from a manifestation of grief and fear to, well, maybe still a manifestation of grief and fear but one that we might also be interested in dating. So how did they make the transition from rotting spectres of disease to hot anti-heroes?

In her 1995 book Our Vampires, Ourselves the late literary scholar Nina Auerbach argued that vampire stories take on the fears and desires of the people telling them. The folk vampires Mahnke described, where dead relatives drain the living and doom a whole family, are one version of that. Another is the predatory aristocrat figure introduced in John Polidori’s 1819 novella The Vampyre—which took cues from his notoriously rakish associate Lord Byron—and then popularized by Bram Stoker in 1897. So what does the influx of cool, sexy vampires say about our current cultural needs? Speaking personally—which I hope you’ll allow me to do since this is more of a question of cultural analysis than empirical research—I think it might have something to do with a shift in what it means to be “other.” The fears that once built monstrous figures like Nosferatu, like xenophobia, still exist especially systemically but are perhaps less popular with mainstream audiences than they were in the 1800s. When Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu published Carmilla in 1872, it was radical in its presentation of a lesbian vampire—but she was also literally a monster. Her otherness was compelling but horrifying. In the latest TV adaptation of Interview with the Vampire, queerness and colorism make the bloodsuckers all the more “other” in the context of their own worlds but actually serve to humanize them for the audience. So maybe our modern vampires reflect a more modern sense of how many of us are the “other” in one way or another.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I spoke about that a bit with Jenny Hamilton, a senior lecturer in counseling and psychological therapy at the University of Lincoln. Her professional work on monsters focuses on how people use them to help process trauma, but she has some thoughts on how monstrous characters have changed with the times. On the one hand, she says, our monsters have shifted from less physical to more psychological in nature as our fears have gotten less primal and more existential.
Jenny Hamilton: In modern and postmodern societies, our anxieties are often less tangible: things like climate change, pandemics, AI, uncertainty about the future.

Feltman: Now, obviously vampires are not the only monster game in town but it makes a lot of sense that being humanoid figures that still engage in very human activities and relationships, they offer a really good template for exploring anxieties that are more social and cultural than physical.

And as figures that sit more firmly on the fuzzy line between human and monster than, say, goblins or dragons, it makes sense that they’ve also been at the forefront of our increasingly complex sense of what makes a monster.
Hamilton: They kind of sit on a lot of boundaries that are a bit difficult for us or taboo. So, you know, the boundaries between life and death, being human and animal.

Feltman: Jenny says that vampires have always been these very contradictory figures who are on the fringes but that our own relationship with the idea of good and bad, villain and hero, is what’s become more nuanced. It’s become more complex as binary traditional ideas about who belongs and who doesn’t have been shed in modern society. In other words, we’ve thankfully come to value a lot of the qualities that used to keep people on the fringes of certain kinds of society.

Now, I’ll pause here to say that of course I know vampires aren’t the only monstrous characters that have gotten the romance treatment, especially in recent years. Just off the top of the dome, I got classic [choices] like Beauty and the Beast, avant-garde ones like The Shape of Water, even zombies thanks to Warm Bodies. We had Lisa Frankenstein, not to mention all of the werewolves in the Twilight franchise and Teen Wolf and similar fiction. We’ve even got that new Olivia Colman movie where she’s married to a big, giant, beautiful man made of wicker, which I cannot wait to see. But I do think vampires are a little unique because most of the other monsters I talked about, you know, they occasionally show up as the love interest in kind of a subversive way. Vampires have become so synonymous with sensuality that, at this point, it’s actually surprising and subversive when a movie makes them gross and not sexy. I’m looking at you, Robert Eggers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But when it comes to how and why we’re able to find literal monsters so attractive, from a purely physical point of view, there’s no clear-cut scientific answer—but there are a lot of really interesting angles to explore.

To get into this I spoke to Mathias Clasen. He’s the co-director of Aarhus University’s Recreational Fear Lab, which is exactly what it sounds like: its mission is to investigate the kinds of things people do because they scare them.

Mathias Clasen: It’s not just watching horror movies.... It’s also some of the earliest playful activities that we expose kids to like, you know, peekaboo, which is a sort of baby jump scare…, running after kids pretending to be a monster. It’s also so-called risky play, you know, kids riding their bikes too fast, climbing trees until they feel butterflies flapping their wings in their stomachs. It’s young women listening to true crime podcasts. It’s middle-aged guys buying fast cars and driving too fast. So there’s a whole range of things people do to get pleasure out of being scared, and that’s what we’re trying to understand.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: Clasen doesn’t currently research our love of monsters, but it’s something he’s thought about a lot.

Clasen: Before, I spent most of my time doing empirical research, like going to haunted attractions to measure the heart rate of guests or try to draw blood samples to look at immune activation, I did a lot of more kind of conceptual theoretical work, including an attempt to explain why monsters are ubiquitous in the landscape of popular culture.
Feltman: One of his favorite examples is the movie Jaws, which led to an actual drop in beach tourism while drawing huge crowds at the theater.

Clasen: The odds of being eaten by a big white shark are, you know, as close to zero as you can get. But there’s something about that monster with the mouth brimming with sharp teeth and the, you know, the dead black eyes that just, I think it triggers something deep within us, and I think that’s what good monsters do, is they trigger, you know, an ancient defense system that evolved way before we were human.

Feltman: Basically, some evolutionary psychologists think that scary play—which includes telling stories about monsters—taps into the same mechanisms for learning and adapting that helped our ancient ancestors survive real threats.

Clasen: We’re kind of hardwired to not just keep our distance but to actually, you know pay attention because that’s the way to learn about different kinds of threats in the environment. So it makes sense that there would be that sort of push-pull ambivalence associated with, you know, monsters and frightening creatures.

And so the reason why there are many more monsters in popular culture than in the real world is that we’re still sort of at the core kind of these cowering, you know, Stone Age hominins, you know, sitting around the bonfire telling stories about all the horrors that exist outside that protective circle of light.
