articles.title: Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer

paras.en: Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer

- Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colonâs protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.

For nearly two decades, scientists have known that a common gut bacterium can produce a toxin that damages the colon and helps drive the formation of tumors. What they could not explain was how the toxin first attaches to intestinal cells and begins its attack. Now, researchers have uncovered that missing step, revealing a surprising vulnerability that could lead to new ways of protecting the colon.

The breakthrough comes from a team led by scientists at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, its Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Their findings, published in Nature, identify a protein called claudin-4 as the essential docking point for a bacterial toxin known as BFT.

Even more promising, the researchers have already used this discovery to develop a molecular decoy that intercepts the toxin before it can damage colon cells. The strategy successfully protected mice from the toxin's harmful effects, suggesting a possible new approach to preventing bacterial damage associated with colorectal cancer. The research received partial support from the National Institutes of Health.

"We've made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment," says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. "Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections."
How a Common Gut Bacterium Can Promote Colon Cancer

The investigation centers on Bacteroides fragilis, a bacterium that can be found in the intestines of up to 20% of healthy people. Although the presence of this bacterium does not automatically mean someone will develop cancer, certain strains produce a powerful toxin capable of disrupting the colon's protective lining, causing inflammation, and encouraging tumor growth.

The toxin, known as B. fragilis toxin or BFT, has been under investigation for years. In a landmark 2009 study published in Nature Medicine, Sears and her colleagues demonstrated that the toxin could promote the development of colon tumors. Their work helped establish an important connection between toxin-producing gut bacteria, chronic inflammation, and colorectal cancer.

Earlier experiments also revealed that BFT damages a protein called E-cadherin, which helps hold neighboring cells together and maintain the colon's protective barrier. When this protein is broken apart, the barrier becomes compromised, potentially allowing harmful substances and bacteria to interfere with the surrounding tissue.

However, one critical question remained unanswered. Although BFT could break down E-cadherin, the toxin did not appear to attach directly to that protein. Researchers suspected that another molecule was helping the toxin reach its target, but repeated attempts to identify it had failed.
Scientists Identify the Missing Link Using CRISPR
To solve the mystery, the researchers turned to CRISPR, a powerful gene-editing technology that allows scientists to selectively disable genes and investigate what they do.

Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate working in Sears' laboratory, led a genome-wide CRISPR screening effort in collaboration with Matthew Waldor's laboratory at Harvard Medical School. The team systematically switched off genes in colon epithelial cells, the cells that form the inner lining of the colon, to determine which ones were necessary for the toxin to attach and cause damage.

One gene stood out dramatically. It produces claudin-4, a protein that helps neighboring cells form tight junctions, the seals that limit the movement of substances between cells and help maintain the intestinal barrier.
When the researchers disabled the gene responsible for claudin-4, BFT could no longer bind to the colon cells. Without that initial attachment, the toxin was unable to attack E-cadherin.
The finding revealed that claudin-4 acts as a receptor for the bacterial toxin. In effect, the toxin must first latch onto this protein before it can carry out its damaging activity.
"It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit," says White. "That was an exciting moment."
An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a New Bacterial Attack Strategy
The identity of the receptor surprised the scientists.

Sears and other researchers had expected BFT to interact with a protein involved in cellular signaling, such as a G protein-coupled receptor. These receptors act somewhat like communication switches, allowing cells to respond to signals from their surroundings.
Claudin-4, however, serves a very different purpose. Rather than functioning primarily as a signaling receptor, it helps maintain the physical connections between neighboring cells.

The discovery also revealed an unusual way for a bacterial toxin to operate. BFT belongs to a class of enzymes called proteases, which cut other proteins. Most proteases act directly on their targets, but BFT appears to require a separate receptor before it can reach and damage E-cadherin.
When the team reviewed previous scientific research, they could not identify another toxin known to use the same mechanism.

To establish that BFT and claudin-4 truly bind to each other, the Johns Hopkins researchers collaborated with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona.

Using techniques that measure how molecules interact, White and the Barcelona team showed that BFT and claudin-4 form a tightly bound complex in laboratory experiments. Each toxin molecule paired with one receptor molecule, providing direct physical evidence of the connection.
A Clever Molecular Decoy Blocks the Dangerous Gut Toxin
Identifying the receptor did more than explain how the toxin works. It also gave the scientists an idea for stopping it.
If BFT needs claudin-4 to attach to colon cells, perhaps a substitute could lure the toxin away from its intended target.

To test that possibility, the team developed a molecular decoy. This was a soluble protein carrying sequences from claudin-4, designed to attract BFT without allowing it to attack the colon's protective lining.

The researchers then worked with Min Dong's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, including Kang Wang and colleagues, to investigate the approach in mice. These experiments allowed the scientists to examine how the toxin behaves in the more complicated environment of a living intestine.

The results were encouraging. Instead of binding to claudin-4 receptors on colon cells, BFT attached to the decoy proteins. By intercepting the toxin, the decoys successfully protected the mice from BFT-induced damage.
The finding suggests that it may be possible to interfere with the toxin's first step rather than trying to repair the damage after it occurs.

"This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties," says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

Small molecules are compounds that can sometimes be developed into medicines, while biologics are treatments made from or involving biological materials, such as proteins. Future versions of the decoy strategy could potentially be designed to work more effectively in the body or be easier to administer.
What This Discovery Could Mean for Colon Cancer Prevention
Although the findings identify a promising new target, important questions remain.

Scientists have established that BFT attaches to claudin-4 and that blocking this interaction can protect mice from toxin-induced damage. However, they have not yet captured the exact experimental three-dimensional structure showing how the two molecules fit together.

Even advanced artificial intelligence tools, including AlphaFold, have been unable to fully resolve the interaction. Understanding its precise structure could help researchers design more effective compounds that prevent the toxin from binding.

Further experiments will also be needed to determine whether the decoy approach can safely and effectively prevent toxin-related disease in humans. The mouse experiments demonstrated protection against tissue damage, but they did not establish that the strategy prevents colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, the discovery resolves a major question that has persisted since the connection between BFT and colon tumor formation was established in 2009. By identifying the toxin's previously unknown point of attachment, researchers have uncovered a potential way to interrupt a harmful biological process before it begins.
The findings could ultimately support new strategies for detecting or treating conditions associated with bacterial toxins, including colorectal cancer, diarrhea, and bloodstream infections.

Additional researchers who contributed to the study include Jason Chen, Shaoguang Wu, Abby L. Geis, and Jessica Queen of Johns Hopkins, along with Hailong Zhang, Karthik Hullahalli, and Jie Zhang of Harvard Medical School.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 31, 2015: Creepy skull-shaped Halloween asteroid flies by Earth, NASA names it the 'Great Pumpkin'
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

paras.en: On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. It arrived with excellent timing on Halloween, which made the already-creepy asteroid even creepier.

During its closest approach, the creepy asteroid was about 300,000 miles from Earth, or 1.3 times the average distance between Earth and the moon. So, it didn't pose a threat to our planet. It was discovered by astronomers at Hawaii's Pan-STARRS observatory only three weeks before the flyby, and it was given the official designation "2015 TB145." But no one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.
NASA called the asteroid the "Great Pumpkin," while others called it the "Halloween Asteroid."
Be afraid, be very afraid... Okay, not really, but there is reason to be concerned about near-Earth objects and the time in which they are detected.

"According to the catalog of near-Earth objects (NEOs) kept by the Minor Planet Center, this is the closest currently known approach by an object this large until asteroid 1999 AN10, at about 2,600 feet (800 meters) in size, approaches at about 1 lunar distance (238,000 miles from Earth) in August 2027," NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) reported in 2015.

NASA’s Near-Earth Object Observations Program, sometimes called “Spaceguard,” works to catalog these type of objects and predicts some of their paths if they could be potentially threats to our planet. While there are no known credible impact threats to date, it doesn't mean the "Great Pumpkin," or rather a great impactor, isn't real.

As for 2015 TB145, it did return to Earth's vicinity in 2018, but at a much more distant pass of about 24 million miles (38 million kilometers), "or about a quarter the distance between Earth and the sun," according to JPL.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

articles.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 234 — Living in Lunar Caves
articles.author: Space.com Staff

paras.en: On Episode 234 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Mike Wall are joined by Than Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute about a NASA-backed payload bound for the Marius Hills Pit on the moon.

In our ongoing quest to develop a moon base, could we possibly utilize the area beneath the surface of the moon in order to make the moon habitable? Could Marius Hills Pit, a roughly 50-meter-wide opening that may lead into a lunar lava tube, become the Moon's first living habitat for humans?

Putzig explains how geophysical instruments on a rover could detect hidden voids beneath the surface and measure the size of these lava tubes. We also ask Than how these lava tubes form, what a follow-up robotic explorer could reveal, and how this research fits alongside NASA’s Artemis plans for a south polar moon base. Join us!
Get episodes ad-free with Club TWiT at https://twit.tv/clubtwit

Finally, did you know you can launch your own SpaceX rocket? Model rocket maker Estes' stunning scale model of a Falcon 9 rocket that you can pick up now. The launchable model is a detailed recreation of the Falcon 9 and retails for $149.99. You can save 10% by using the code IN-COLLECTSPACE at checkout, courtesy of our partners collectSPACE.com.

This Week in Space covers the new space age. Every Friday we take a deep dive into a fascinating topic. What's happening with the new race to the moon and other planets? When will SpaceX really send people to Mars?

Rod Pyle is an author, journalist, television producer and Editor-in-Chief of Ad Astra magazine. He has written 18 books on space history, exploration, and development, including Space 2.0, Innovation the NASA Way, Interplanetary Robots, Blueprint for a Battlestar, Amazing Stories of the Space Age, First On the Moon, and Destination Mars

In a previous life, Rod produced numerous documentaries and short films for The History Channel, Discovery Communications, and Disney. He also worked in visual effects on Star Trek: Deep Space Nine and the Battlestar Galactica reboot, as well as various sci-fi TV pilots. His most recent TV credit was with the NatGeo documentary on Tom Wolfe's iconic book The Right Stuff.

Responsible for Space.com's editorial vision, Tariq Malik has been the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com since 2019 and has covered space news and science for 18 years. He joined the Space.com team in 2001, first as an intern and soon after as a full-time spaceflight reporter covering human spaceflight, exploration, astronomy and the night sky. He became Space.com's managing editor in 2009. As on-air talent has presented space stories on CNN, Fox News, NPR and others.

Tariq is an Eagle Scout (yes, he earned the Space Exploration merit badge), a Space Camp veteran (4 times as a kid, once as an adult), and has taken the ultimate "vomit comet" ride while reporting on zero-gravity fires. Before joining Space.com, he served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering city and education beats. He has journalism degrees from the University of Southern California and New York University.

Space.com is the premier source of space exploration, innovation and astronomy news, chronicling (and celebrating) humanity's ongoing expansion across the final frontier. Originally founded in 1999, Space.com is, and always has been, the passion of writers and editors who are space fans and also trained journalists. Our current news team consists of Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik; Editor Hanneke Weitering, Senior Space Writer Mike Wall; Senior Writer Meghan Bartels; Senior Writer Chelsea Gohd, Senior Writer Tereza Pultarova and Staff Writer Alexander Cox, focusing on e-commerce. Senior Producer Steve Spaleta oversees our space videos, with Diana Whitcroft as our Social Media Editor.

articles.title: 9 nightmarish sci-fi spaceships to crawl aboard for Halloween if you dare
articles.author: Jeff Spry

paras.en: Abandoned, possessed, or infested spaceships in sci-fi films, books, and video games are usually not a welcoming place to hang your helmet and kick back inside.

Many are distinctly marked as DO NOT APPROACH zones and equipped with clearly articulated warning messages to keep your distance, but that doesn't ever seem to stop scavengers, space pirates, or evil industrial mega corporations from waving off these dangerous signs to board anyway.

Other creaky craft are apt to contain nasty alien hitchhikers or biological hazards not exactly conducive to a pleasant star-trekking voyage. Whether these nefarious neglected craft have just reappeared from the other side of a black hole or have been lying dormant for eons on a hostile planetoid, visitors are usually infrequent.
So ignore those distress beacons at your own peril and step into this alarming armada of 9 nightmarish sci-fi spaceships before orbits decay.
It's basically a perfectly good interstellar mining vessel owned by the Concordance Extraction Corporation if you forget about the nasty reanimated corpses found lurking on nearly every deadly deck.
The pesky Necromorphs are a resilient crop of creatures and are extremely inhospitable when it comes to having uninvited guests, yet they don't mind if you're staying for dinner.
This plague of hungry zombified corpses is a real drag, unless you happen to have a flaring plasma cutter in your back pocket and your name is Isaac Clarke.

Things would be much more peaceful aboard the Grendel if a notorious undead slasher named Jason Voorhees wasn't stashed in the cargo bay, but when scientific discovery enters the equation, many questionable choices follow.

The Grendel is a 25th-century medical research vessel on a field trip from hell to an overly polluted Earth, where the frozen Jason is kept at the Crystal Lake Research Facility and shipped back home to Earth 2 for cellular research.
Once thawed, the ship becomes his private killing field with an ample supply of student bodies until the fiery finale when Jason becomes an inhuman meteor in the sky. Next time, take the school bus.
This spooky classic novel written by "2001's" legendary author, Arthur C. Clarke, focuses on a massive alien spaceship entering Earth's atmosphere.

The 31-mile-long cylindrical spaceship does not parallel park easily and is quite spacious inside. In fact, it’s primarily hollow at first and likely offers up a fantastic location for some echoey yodeling. As we later learn, Rama aliens are apparently collecting forms of intelligent life from around the galaxy, employing their ginormous Rama spacecraft.

As an ice ring thaws and forms a vast ocean, astronauts explore the ship’s cavernous confines, only to find automated bio-machines and weird metallic towers, curved alloy cliffs, and fantastic geometric city-like structures. The myriad mysteries that unfold are enough to drive sane humans to absolute madness!
4. THE SCOPULI — "LEVIATHAN WAKES" (2011)

Ignore that glistening brown protomolecular goo, and come on in and sit a spell in the Scopuli, a light Martian freighter used by the Outer Planets Alliance for clandestine missions and ransacked by the evil security firm Protogen in an attempt to hijack its alien cargo.

Hailing from James S.A. Corey's first book in "The Expanse Series", the Scopuli was found moored to an asteroid by James Holden and his Canterbury crew. The amber-brown mess discovered inside the rigged ship is not to be trifled with, let alone inhaled, eaten, or touched.
Come to think of it, it’s probably much wiser to get out while you can and move along!

Anything that looks like an organic hammer-headed horseshoe lying canted in a rocky ravine on a hostile, uncharted planetoid is best to avoid. Especially when its repeating SOS beacon is translated into its true message… a dire warning to keep curious rubberneckers the hell away!

Once its strange, sexually suggestive openings are penetrated by Nostromo crew members, seeing fossilized giants and oceans of squishy egg pods in the cargo hold would make most reasonable people flee in terror.
We're better off leaving this sleeping nightmare in its resting place.
6. CHALLENGE 142 — "IT, THE TERROR FROM BEYOND SPACE" (1956)

One of the inspirations for Ridley Scott's "Alien", this Golden Age goodie brings us aboard the sleek silver rescue rocketship, Challenge 142, and locks us inside after a bloodthirsty reptilian alien from Mars decides to catch a lift back to Earth with its new astronaut friends in the far-flung future of... 1973!

Mute, clawed monsters with insatiable appetites for human flesh are never good travel companions in the confines of a steel spacecraft. A wiser choice would have been to have stayed on Mars and used the Challenge 142 as a stylized red planet potato farm.
Need a glowing golden suntan? This vessel was launched from Earth to detonate a nuclear payload within the sun's fury to keep its fusion furnace burning and was never heard from again.

A sister rescue vessel, the Icarus 2, was dispatched as a last resort and encountered this long-abandoned ship drifting near the scorching star. Inside the Icarus 1, its over-tanned Captain Pinback has been caught in an addictive ritual of basking in the sun's brilliant embrace and has gone quite insane.
Back out quietly and toss him a nice bottle of aloe vera lotion.
8. THE EVENT HORIZON — "EVENT HORIZON" (1997)
Lawrence Fishburne's Captain Miller thinks this place is a tomb! Well, that's not a very polite way to describe what I think is one of the most ominous spaceships ever seen on screen.

The fact that this foreboding vessel, designed after the cathedral of Notre Dame, has appeared in Neptune's orbit following its disappearance after entering a black hole should be enough to keep the crew of the Lewis and Clark from steering anywhere close. Nothing good can be happening on that doomed craft considering the seven-year absence.

One second after discovering that the craft punctured a route straight to Hades and returned with some extra baggage, I'd be running for the exit hatch! The welcome mat is out, but there's no need to knock on this airlock.

Basically an "Alien" ripoff, this low-budget cult sci-fi flick has its following, but only from those midnight runs to the video store in the '80s to grab the tape with the craziest-looking alien on the cover.

The Shenandoah is a prospecting explorer sent by a ruthless corporation to claim an alien archaeological site on Saturn's moon, Titan. Assorted chaos ensues when a rival West German spaceship is discovered at the dig site, only for our protagonists to find the crew slaughtered.

The carnivorous monster that creeps onto the Shenandoah suffers from little monster syndrome, but its bite is impressive. Best to have never touched the metallic pods in the subterranean cave and just skipped this homicidal mission entirely.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

articles.title: Craft Prospect kicks off PERSEUS project to advance optical communications for space
articles.author: Craft Prospect

paras.en: Craft Prospect is working with Fraunhofer Centre for Applied Photonics (Fraunhofer CAP) and Vector Photonics on a new project exploring the potential of next-generation laser technology for high-performance optical communications in space.

PERSEUS (PCSEL Environmental and Radiation Sensitivity: Evaluation for Use in Space) will investigate whether a promising new laser technology called Photonic-Crystal Surface-Emitting Lasers (PCSELs) is suitable for operation in space and can offer a differentiated capability for both space-to-space and space/ground networks.

The project will evaluate the technology under conditions relevant to space deployment, demonstrate its compatibility with representative spacecraft hardware, and identify the next engineering steps required to move towards a commercial solution.

The project is funded through the Advanced Connectivity Technologies (ACT) programme, delivered by Innovate UK and funded by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The ACT R&D Programme was announced by Minister Ian Murray during his speech at Connected Britain on 9 September 2026.
Exploring a new approach to optical communications

PCSEL technology offers the potential to address some of the limitations of existing optical and RF communications systems in space, supporting the move towards longer-range, higher-capacity, and more secure free-space optical links between ground stations, satellites, and potentially deeper-space assets.
By bridging the gap between component and space system, PERSEUS will chart a course from disruptive technology to differentiated on-orbit capability for the fast-growing space market.
From device testing to spacecraft integration

The PERSEUS programme will subject PCSELs to a range of test campaigns expected of space qualified technologies, as well as carrying out long-range, high-bandwidth free-space demonstrations to showcase early performance.

PCSEL devices will undergo characterisation and testing, including radiation, vibration, and thermal-vacuum campaigns, to better our understanding of how the technology fares in the launch and space environments.

Furthermore, the project will demonstrate early integration success with other flight-representative hardware for end-to-end data transmission, and develop mission concepts that harness the unique capabilities of PCSELs.

The findings will feed into a future communications system design concept and help define the engineering roadmap required to progress PCSEL technology towards a differentiated space communications solution.
Bringing together photonics and space engineering expertise
At Craft Prospect, Head of Engineering Kevin Quillien is serving as Project Lead, supported by Chief Engineer Paul Yarr and Systems Engineers Lauryn Atkinson and Kairavi Pandit.
At Fraunhofer CAP, Dr Gerald Bonner is subcontract lead, while at Vector Photonics Dr Richard Taylor serves as subcontract lead and Dr Graham Goldberg as Project Manager.

The project also builds on Craft Prospect’s growing quantum-optical communications capability, including our work on OPS-SAT VOLT, where we are developing and testing space-to-ground free-space quantum and optical communications technologies as part of our wider mission to deliver Smart Secure Space.
Kevin Quillien, Project Lead and Head of Engineering Craft Prospect, said of the project:
‘PERSEUS is an exciting opportunity to take a promising new photonics technology and understand the potential it has to offer the space industry.

‘By carrying out all the necessary early-stage work to test and characterise PCSELs for space, we will build a strong understanding of the potential that the technology offers in building the next generation of communication solutions. We’re looking forward to working with Fraunhofer CAP and Vector Photonics to explore where this roadmap will take us.’

Craft Prospect is a Glasgow-based space engineering company advancing its vision of Smart Secure Space through onboard intelligence, quantum technologies, and satellite subsystem innovation. Learn more here.
About Fraunhofer Centre for Applied Photonics

Fraunhofer CAP is a not-for-profit research and technology organisation (RTO) offering industry a professional development capability in the fields of photonics, lasers and quantum technologies. Learn more about Fraunhofer CAP here.

Vector Photonics Limited, based in Glasgow, is advancing its revolutionary, proprietary, PCSEL technology from proven R&D and commercial fab environments to high-volume manufacturing. Further information can be found here

articles.title: Millwall ease past sorry Derby as Lisbie nets twice

paras.en: Millwall vs Derby County; Sky Bet Championship
Millwall vs Derby County. Sky Bet Championship.
Millwall 4-1 Derby County: Kyrell Lisbie scores twice in Lions win

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Millwall and Derby County at The Den on Saturday; Kyrell Lisbie scores twice as the Lions romp past John Eustace’s struggling Rams.
Kyrell Lisbie scored twice in the early stages as Millwall eased to a 4-1 victory against struggling Derby at The Den in the Sky Bet Championship.
The Lions roared out of the blocks as they scored three goals in the first 17 minutes to ensure what was just their second win in eight league games was secured with plenty to spare.
This was another worrying afternoon for the Rams, though, who were never in the contest and they remain second from bottom, four points from safety, and without a win in nine games.

Millwall were ahead after only three minutes when Camiel Neghli passed inside to Lyndon Dykes whose own ball found Lisbie in plenty of space and the winger placed his shot into the bottom corner via a slight deflection.
The lead was doubled in the 10th minute, though, when Neghli bent in an excellent cross from the left and Dykes' header across the six-yard box gave Lisbie the easiest of tap-ins.
Derby had a great chance to pull a goal back quickly, but their captain Carlton Morris skied his effort after being found at the back post by Rhian Brewster's low cross.

Instead, Millwall had their third with only 17 minutes on the clock when Neghli's ball over the top allowed Luke Cundle to run in behind a flat-footed defence and finish well past the helpless Jacob Widell Zetterstrom.
The Rams' goalkeeper could be forgiven what was going on in front of him, while the away supporters were singing "you're not fit to wear the shirt" at their own players.
Derby almost registered within a minute of the restart when Sam Szmodics fizzed the ball across the box and Morris' header was clawed behind by Millwall goalkeeper Max Crocombe.

The visitors were looking far more coherent - in contrast to their desperate start to proceedings - but were struggling to create clear-cut chances, with Brewster shooting at Crocombe from a narrow angle.

Cundle almost had his second of the afternoon for the Lions when his shot was beaten away by Zetterstrom before Caleb Taylor headed over for the hosts after Derek Mazou-Sacko's cross ricocheted into his path.
Mihaiolo Ivanovic then set up his fellow sub, Romain Esse, who should have added a fourth when his scuffed effort was kept out by Zetterstrom.

But extra gloss was added to the scoreline in the 84th minute when Alfie Doughty's mishit shot from distance ran for Ivanovic who unselfishly squared the ball for captain Jake Cooper to slam into the roof of the net.
Derby, at least, struck a consolation with three minutes left when Filip Bilbija fired in his first goal for the club after Crocombe had kept out a shot from Oscar Fraulo.

articles.title: Lankshear scores twice in Boro win

paras.en: Middlesbrough vs Charlton Athletic; Sky Bet Championship
Middlesbrough vs Charlton Athletic. Sky Bet Championship.
Middlesbrough 3-0 Charlton Athletic: Will Lankshear scores twice in Boro win

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Middlesbrough and Charlton Athletic at the Riverside Stadium on Saturday; Will Lankshear scores twice in a comfortable win for the league leaders.
In-form Will Lankshear bagged a brace as Middlesbrough maintained their position at the Championship summit with a comprehensive 3-0 victory over Charlton at the Riverside.
Sebastian Berhalter opened the scoring in the 12th minute before Lankshear netted twice to take his tally to 15 in all competitions.

While the early exchanges were not without the odd nervy moment for a home side who came into the match unbeaten in their last 10 league matches, a long throw into the Boro box led to a quick counter and a shot from the division's top scorer Lankshear, resulting in a corner.

Charlton's Tyler Bindon picked up a yellow card inside 10 minutes for a late challenge and the resulting free-kick led to a header into the side-netting from Riley McGree, which seemed to give the home team and supporters a lift.

The first goal came shortly after, with the tricky feet of Amario Cozier-Duberry on the right ensuring he found enough space to pull the back to the edge of the 18-yard box for Berhalter, who produced a tidy finish to the goalkeeper's right. Arthur Okonkwo may well feel he could have done better, however.
Charlton went on to produce a couple of half-chances themselves, including a close-range shot from a wide angle from Joe Rankin-Costello, which was comfortably saved by Radek Vitek.

A deep cross from Cozier-Duberry then found the ever-dangerous Tommy Conway all on his own at the back post, but his curling shot went narrowly wide, while just after the half-hour mark a long Charlton throw was headed goalwards by Miles Leaburn and had Vitek scrambling, but missed the target.
McGree was given a deserved yellow for a heavy challenge on Charlton's Kayne Ramsay in the opposition box after losing control of the ball, with Ramsay having to be replaced at half-time.

The second goal came shortly before the break, with Berhalter producing a sumptuous through ball to find Lankshear. Cries of offside from the away side were ignored by the linesman and Lankshear produced a tidy dink finish to double the lead.

Charlton had a couple of threatening moments at the start of the second half, but Middlesbrough soon took control, with a McGree shot over the bar followed by a curling strike from Cozier-Duberry that looked destined for the top corner but went narrowly wide.
After a couple of dangerous looking crosses from Middlesbrough captain Callum Brittain that were begging to be converted, the victory was finally sealed in the 82nd minute.

Within seconds of being introduced from the bench, Charlton's Nathaniel Chalobah slipped on the edge of his own box and the ball dropped kindly to Lankshear, whose left-foot strike emphatically found the top corner, taking his league tally to 13 goals in as many games.
Lankshear was replaced immediately afterwards with what looked like cramp, with another excellent afternoon's work done and dusted.

articles.title: U.K. PM open to slave trade apology but rules out financial reparations
articles.author: Freddie Clayton

paras.en: LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to a formal apology for his country’s role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations as King Charles III continued his tour of the Caribbean.
Burnham’s comments show a marked shift in stance for the U.K., which has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
They came as he is due to attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week. Charles, as head of the “family of nations,” will preside over the event.

“We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade,” Burnham wrote in an op-ed in The Guardian newspaper published Friday. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”
But Burnham ruled out financial reparations, saying the British people of today who “played no personal part” in the slave trade could not be held liable.

The trans-Atlantic trade in enslaved people was central to European colonialism and the growth of the British Empire, as millions of Africans were trafficked to the Americas to grow and harvest cash crops, while being subjected to violence, torture, sexual abuse and the denial of basic human rights.
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said on X that he welcomed the prime minister’s openness to a formal apology.
Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also posted on X, writing: “Open-minded dialogue is always a good place to start addressing difficult issues.”
Jamaica recently took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal.
Caribbean nations had urged Britain to acknowledge its role in the slave trade ahead of Charles’ visit to the Bahamas and Guyana last week.
Charles last week visited Clifford Park, where in 1973 he granted the Bahamas independence after 300 years of British rule.
Members of the Bahamas’ Rastafarian community and others lined a nearby road to protest.
“Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against Black people.”

In his first public remarks on the island nation, Charles said: “It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present.”

articles.title: ‘Looks like Mars’: Toxic smog from Indonesia wildfires sparks health crisis, protests
articles.author: Tavleen Tarrant

paras.en: Almost every day for months, Indonesian schoolteacher Natanael Undas has gazed up at smoke-filled skies in apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange.

“It looks like Mars, like we’re living on another planet,” said Undas, whose home in central Kalimantan province is at the heart of devastating wildfires generating toxic smog in Indonesia and across Southeast Asia.

Although his family keeps the windows shut at all times, the noxious smoke penetrates the house anyway, sending Undas’ 2-year-old daughter into constant sneezing fits amid a spike in respiratory illnesses in haze-affected regions.

Wildfires are nothing new in Indonesia, whose forests and peatlands are set ablaze each year as family and commercial farms clear land using traditional “slash and burn” methods. But the fires this year are far worse than usual, said Undas, who has been documenting Indonesia’s air quality on Instagram since 2014, as heat and drought aggravated by a “super” El Niño weather pattern make this the country’s worst fire season in over a decade.
Wildfire smoke covers Indonesia skies in orange haze

The unrelenting haze from the fires has affected millions of people in the region since they started in July, closing schools in multiple countries and spurring arguments about who is to blame. Indonesian protesters have accused their government of insufficient action, while other countries are threatening prosecution.

On Wednesday, hundreds of Indonesian students and members of civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against the policies of President Prabowo Subianto, including his resistance to declaring the fires a national disaster.
“We want transparent and independent investigations about these wildfires,” protester Natasha Ruvantina told NBC News. “And also, we want a long-term prevention strategy.”
The Indonesian government said in a statement Wednesday that it recognized the students’ concerns, adding that it was prosecuting companies linked to the fires and sending aid to affected provinces.

The fires have also caused frustration in countries such as neighboring Singapore, where air pollution this month reached its highest level since 2015, when Indonesian wildfires were also intensified by El Niño. Singapore officials have threatened to prosecute companies seen as responsible for the devastation, and on Tuesday the foreign ministers of Singapore and Indonesia said they were considering a joint task force to combat illegal land burning.
“We will use the full force of the law to make sure those who profit from fire must answer for the fires,” Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said.
Indonesia’s neighbors and other countries have been accused of contributing to the problem.

In a report this month, the Indonesian environmental organization Walhi named 66 companies with links to Singapore and 27 companies with links to Malaysia that it said were associated with fire hot spots. On Thursday, the Indonesian government said police had identified 20 corporations suspected of being involved in the fires, including four from Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea.
The Malaysian government has denied that any Malaysian companies are involved, while the government of Singapore did not respond to a request for comment.

Even as fingers are pointed across borders, the fires have been causing disruptions across the region, even threatening 67,000-year-old cave paintings on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi that are the oldest in the world.
The haze also marred Singapore’s annual Formula One night race this month, obscuring the city’s iconic skyline during the globally watched event.
“The biggest issue is a change in the quality of life,” Rajasekhar Balasubramanian, an engineering professor at the National University of Singapore, said of the haze.
“People who usually participate in outdoor activities, for example, doing some kind of physical exercise, cannot do it anymore,” he said.

A Singapore-focused study published in September found that short-term increases in airborne fine particulate matter were associated with increased emergency department visits for asthma and other chronic respiratory illnesses. According to the study, spikes in such visits in 2016 and 2019 coincided with periods of haze caused by Indonesian wildfires.

In Indonesia, more than 283,000 cases of respiratory illness linked to the current fires had been reported in seven provinces as of Oct. 13, more than double the 113,000 cases reported as of Sept. 9, Reuters reported, citing Health Ministry data.
Adeline Tong, a civil engineer in Singapore, said that the recent haze had brought back her long-dormant asthma and that if she goes outside without an N95 mask, “I will feel like I need my inhaler.”
“Just two days ago, I could not even see the condo next to mine. It disappeared because the visibility was so bad,” she said in an interview on Oct. 21.

While Tong is able to work remotely, she said the haze has affected her social life, discouraging her from meeting friends at the outdoor food courts and hawker stalls that are ubiquitous in Singapore.
It has also affected her as a competitive ballroom dancer, she said.
“I usually would run outside to train, but now I can’t do that because the outside air will make me feel worse and the gyms are so crowded now because no one is outside,” she said.

For many others — including the scores of Indigenous tribes living in Borneo, an island divided among Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei where the fires are concentrated — staying indoors isn’t an option.

Molly Wang and Marianna Madun are Penans, a seminomadic, hunter-gatherer tribe indigenous to Sarawak, a Malaysian state in Borneo near the fires in Kalimantan, the Indonesian part of the island. They live in a village of around 150 people in Sarawak’s Baram region, where they weave baskets and bags for a living.

Wang said the fires and smoke had sent animals running deeper into the jungle, making it harder for the community to hunt, while Madun said gathering food had been difficult because the smoke irritates her eyes.
The community has also paused traditional slash-and-burn farming techniques to avoid adding more smoke to the air.
Wang said that while she doesn’t feel major health effects, older community members have been coughing and having trouble breathing; the closest clinic is an hour away by motorbike.
Despite deploying thousands of personnel, Indonesia has struggled to quell the fires, which include vegetation fires above ground, as well as peat fires below.

Peat fires “are very difficult to put out and continue to smolder for ages,” Balasubramanian said. “So when you have ripe, dry conditions, a small little incident could ignite wildfires above the surface, and it’s very hard to control.”

Though the fires are expected to continue into early November because of a delayed rainy season, smaller showers this week have brought some relief, with firefighters in Indonesia dancing in delight and residents across the region celebrating the first “blue sky” days in weeks.

articles.title: Canada hoping to become EU’s first 'associate member' in deal

paras.en: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is expecting to finalise an agreement for Canada to become the European Union's first "associate member" by June.
Leaders from both sides have wrapped up a two-day summit in Montreal focused on forging closer economic and security ties.
Canadian cabinet ministers and European commissioners will meet in March ahead of concluding negotiations on the proposed alliance at European Council meetings in June.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is hoping to wrap up an unprecedented deal with the European Union by June to make Canada the bloc's first "associate member".

Mr Carney and EU leaders launched what they called an "Alliance for the Future" at the end of a two-day Canada-EU summit in Montreal where they agreed to several initiatives centred on digital trade, critical minerals and artificial intelligence among others.
"Today we move toward associate membership for Canada, and we launch a new alliance for the future,"
US President Donald Trump's trade war and persistent threats have accelerated efforts by Canada and Europe to reduce their dependence on Washington and strengthen their economic and security ties.
"What brings us together goes far beyond geography. We see the world through the same eyes," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"These headwinds won't stop blowing. This change is permanent."
Mr Carney said the alliance would help Canada and Europe withstand economic pressure and make their own decisions rather than be dictated to by more powerful countries.
Mr Trump has threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered the proposed arrangement unfriendly.
Mr Carney did not directly say whether the US could eventually be invited to join the alliance, but insisted the arrangement was not retaliatory.

"It is about reinforcing sovereignty. Why? So we can live our lives as we choose, our people can live their lives as they choose and have the full freedoms that people enjoy in the European Union and in Canada," Mr Carney said.

Mr Carney said Canadian Cabinet ministers and European commissioners would meet in March before he attends European Council meetings in June, where he intends to conclude negotiations on the proposed relationship.
European Council President António Costa confirmed the invitation and said more details would be announced then.
Ms Von der Leyen said on Friday there was broad support for bringing Canada closer to the EU.
"On one thing I'm absolutely sure, having spoken about it in the last weeks, is the broad support of having Canada much, much closer to the European Union," she said.
Friday's negotiations in Montreal produced a new digital trade agreement between Canada and the EU to make it easier for businesses to sell across the Atlantic.
Canada also signed an agreement allowing the European Investment Bank to finance Canadian critical minerals projects, potentially opening a new source of investment for the country's mining industry.

Canada will also join a European supercomputing initiative which Mr Carney said could transform research. Europe's JUPITER supercomputer can complete in one day calculations that would take Canada's most powerful research computer six months, he said.
The two sides also concluded negotiations on an agreement intended to curb anti-competitive practices and lower prices for consumers.
The Alliance for the Future could eventually broaden to include other like-minded countries, with Canada and the EU at its core.
Mr Costa said the two sides wanted to create a relationship unlike any seen previously with a country outside the bloc.
"Our relationship is so special that we want to create something new: to go beyond a simple association, everything short of full EU membership," he said.
The leaders also agreed to study the feasibility of exporting Canadian liquefied natural gas to Europe and explore new undersea cables connecting Canada, Europe and Asia.
Canada and the EU will begin talks on expanding Canadian participation in Europe's student exchange program.
The two sides also agreed on a new border security arrangement and pledged closer cooperation on defence, cybersecurity, Arctic security and countering foreign interference.
The US accounted for 71.7 per cent of Canada's merchandise exports in 2025. Mr Carney wants to double exports to other countries over the next decade.

articles.title: Iranian military ordered to counter any attack swiftly and without restraint
articles.author: Laura Tingle

paras.en: Iran's Supreme Leader Mjotaba Khamenei has ordered his military chiefs to meet any attack on Iran with an immediate and unrestrained response.
The orders indicate that Iran would broaden the targets it strikes from predominantly military ones.
It comes after four oil tankers hit mines and caught fire while travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has issued new strategic orders to his military chiefs that they should respond to any military or terrorist attack on Iran with an "immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response".

The orders suggest Iran is prepared to widen the war across the region — and possibly further — if the US and Israel launch a new attack on Iran, further alarming Gulf countries which came under attacks from Iran earlier in the year and which have been urging the United States not to restart conflict with Iran.
The message outlining the orders, which appeared on Khamenei's X account also "expressed his appreciation for the intelligent steadfastness of the Resistance Front in various countries".
The Resistance Front is an Islamist militant organisation and proxy group operating in Jammu and Kashmir.
Mr Khamenei described the "unity of fronts" as a decisive factor with a strategic impact on shaping the new political and security order in West Asia.

Iran's military chiefs have also been ordered to update the "Targets Bank" so that all kinds of tangible and intangible assets of the US and Israel would be within the reach of the armed forces, his statement said.
The orders indicate that Iran would broaden the targets it strikes from predominantly military ones, and that it would instruct its satellite organisations — Hezbollah and Hamas — to also engage.

The orders were issued as reports from Washington suggested US gulf allies had been warned to expect a new assault on Iran as early as Wednesday, November 4, immediately after the US mid-term elections.
The New York Times reported last week that the US and Israel have drawn up joint plans to attack Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections.
Qatar has been attempting to broker negotiations between Iran and the United States, first in meetings in Tehran and now in Doha.
Despite suggestions that representatives from Iran and the US would come to Doha for direct talks, it subsequently emerged that there were no US representatives in Doha for the meetings.
Both the US and Iran have been ramping up their rhetoric in the days leading up to the US midterm elections, due to be held on Monday.

And Mr Khamenei's threats came after it was reported that that the head of United States Central Command (CENTCOM) Admiral Brad Cooper had briefed Mr Trump on options for renewed attacks on attacking Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal.

At the same time,The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance had offered to meet Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, in person to negotiate an end to the war.

Saudi Arabia and Türkiye's leaders have urged Trump to give diplomacy with Iran more time, while Netanyahu is lobbying for a joint US-Israeli military operation against Iran immediately after the US midterm elections.
Efforts to open dialogue with Iran 'a positive step'

In an interview with Al Jazeera, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that a US effort to open dialogue with Iran is "a positive step", and that talks with Qatari mediators have resulted in reducing the period required to implement Iran's proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz.

"The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days," said Mr Araghchi.

"Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region. We demand the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all our frozen funds, including those held in Qatar," Mr Araghchi added.
He said his country does not rule out the possibility of an attack against Iran.
"We do not rule out any possibility regarding the outbreak of war, and we are prepared for all scenarios," Mr Araghchi said.
"We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms; our forces are at the highest level of readiness."
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says four oil tankers, including a "supertanker" carrying more than two million barrels of oil, hit mines and caught fire while travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said the tankers suffered explosions on Friday after attempting to use unauthorised routes through the strait.

The Guard's navy claimed the vessels had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and ignored repeated radio warnings. Iran's report did not identify the vessels or provide details about the crews.

Oman said it had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked in the strait, 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam Governorate, catching fire. It is unclear whether that incident is related to the fires described by Iran.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre also reported on Friday that a vessel was struck by an "unknown projectile" south of Lavan, an island just off mainland Iran near Shidvar.
The British military organisation, which monitors maritime safety, said the crew was safe.
An Iranian official said two fishermen were missing and two others injured in an attack on two other boats in the strait, blaming the US.
Iran has repeatedly warned that vessels passing through the strait without Tehran's permission would face "destruction."
Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28.

articles.title: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Ukraine amid ceasefire

paras.en: Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have arrived in Ukraine.
It comes amid the Kherson region localised ceasefire, the most significant truce since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The ceasefire is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have reached Ukraine under the most significant truce since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, which the White House says was brokered with help from US first lady Melania Trump, began at 3am local time on Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
It was a rare joint Russia-Ukraine humanitarian effort, a brief respite in the grim war.
Civilians from Oleshky, on the Dnipro River, began the long journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said those who chose to travel from Oleshky to Ukrainian-held territory were taken to the Russian city of Anapa and flown to the Belarusian city of Homel.
They were accompanied by Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, it said.

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the US first lady posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Reunions after some families separated for over two years
Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them.
Volunteers from organisations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.
Liza Paliy, who last saw her father over two years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbours but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realised that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

articles.title: This Texas midterm race has huge stakes, both for Donald Trump and the country
articles.author: Mike Crawley

paras.en: This Texas midterm race has huge stakes, both for Donald Trump and the country
Republican Ken Paxton is struggling to hold state that hasn't sent Democrat to U.S. Senate since 1988
In the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, no race has more at stake than the battle to become the next senator for Texas.

The contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico matters for Americans across the U.S., as the outcome could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate for the remainder of Donald Trump’s presidency.
"If we lose Texas, we're going to lose the country," Paxton has told the Republican faithful at numerous campaign rallies.
The stakes are particularly significant for Trump, since all the reasons the Republicans risk losing in Texas trace directly back to him.
Trump pointedly inserted himself into the Texas race from the start by endorsing the scandal-ridden Paxton to become the Republican candidate over long-serving incumbent Sen. John Cornyn.

Paxton's sketchy ethical record, high prices for gas and diesel triggered by Trump's war on Iran and heavy-handed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics are all driving what appears to be a dramatic shift in voter sentiment.

No Texas Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate since 1988, the year before Talarico was born. Despite that history, and despite Trump carrying Texas by 13 percentage points just two years ago, polling averages suggest a Democrat win this time is a distinct possibility.

Paxton's campaign is based on low taxes, cracking down on illegal immigration and supporting Trump's agenda. Talarico's key themes include stopping cuts to health-care funding, imposing term limits on members of Congress and shifting the tax burden from the middle class to corporations and the wealthy.
Both candidates have described the consequences of the election in monumental terms, frequently depicting their opponent as extreme.
The race "isn't just red versus blue," Paxton told a recent rally in the Dallas suburb of Allen. "It's the America our founders gave us versus something they would never recognize.”
"Ken Paxton is everything that's wrong with our politics," countered Talarico later that same day at a rally in Fort Worth. "We are running against the most corrupt politician in Texas."

The corruption cloud hanging over Paxton, the state's attorney general since 2015, includes a grand jury indictment for securities fraud and impeachment in the Texas House for abusing his office to help a political donor. (The fraud charge was eventually dropped after he struck a plea deal, and the Texas Senate declined to convict following his impeachment.)

Voters attend a joint midterm election rally in Weslaco, Tex. on Oct. 25 for three Democratic Party candidates: James Talarico for the U.S. Senate, Bobby Pulido for the U.S. House and Gina Hinojosa for state governor. (Michael Gonzalez/The Associated Press)
Paxton casts Talarico — a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who has served in the state legislature since 2019 — as a dangerous, leftist radical.

"A vote for James Talarico is not just a vote for his radical agenda," Paxton told the Allen rally. "It's a vote for every dangerous idea that Democrats across the country are putting forward right now.”
Paxton's backers go even further in their rhetoric.
Lydia Elizondo, the Republican running for district attorney in the South Texas county of Hidalgo County, introduced Paxton at a rally last week.
"We cannot let evil win," Elizondo told the crowd. "That evil has a name, and its name is James Talarico."
- Cross Country Checkup is asking: How will the U.S. midterm elections affect you? What questions do you have? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show
One tangible sign of the high stakes: The Senate race in Texas is poised to become the single-most expensive non-presidential campaign in U.S. history.

Spending on advertising by the candidates, parties and corporate-funded political action committees since the Texas primaries began has surpassed $500 million US, according to data compiled by the firm AdImpact.
Much of that spending has been bankrolled by one rich Texas resident who also happens to be the wealthiest man on Earth.
Two of Elon Musk's political action committees have funneled more than $210 million US to help the Paxton campaign, according to election finance filings.
The Musk-funded ads are primarily aimed at motivating Republicans to vote by invoking culture-war fears about the consequences of a Talarico win.

One ad claims Talarico wants "taxpayer-funded sex-change surgeries on kids." Another claims he backs "putting parents in jail if they do not support surgically transitioning their children." Talarico has rejected the accusations as lies.
The Democrat has in turn made Musk's investments in the Paxton campaign part of his argument to voters.
"Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat," Talarico said as the Fort Worth crowd booed the name of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO.
James Talarico, the Democrat candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, speaks at a campaign rally in Fort Worth on Oct. 19. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
"But on November 3rd, we will deliver a crystal-clear message to the world's first trillionaire. We will let Elon Musk know that Texas is not for sale."
Advance turnout figures provide some evidence the Democrats' messaging may be working more effectively than the Republicans'.

During the first week of early voting in Texas, people who'd previously voted in a Democratic Party primary slightly outnumbered those who'd voted in a Republican primary, a scenario that a Republican political consultant described as unprecedented.

At a polling station in the South Texas city of Edinburg, first-time voter Laysha Chavez said the key factor driving her decision was the way ICE deportations have separated families who've lived in the U.S. for many years.
"Seeing that happen really breaks my heart because you never know who it could be next. It could be your friend; it could someone close to you," Chavez, a biology student, told CBC News.
There's a range of polling evidence suggesting that Hispanic voters in Texas, who swung toward Trump in record numbers in 2024, have soured on Republicans in 2026.
Also in Edinburg last week, Paxton drew around 100 people to an evening rally, including Ruben Martinez, who said he supports the Republican Party in part for how it deals with illegal immigration.

"It's like, right now here, we're waiting in line to get in," Martinez told CBC News outside the venue. "So it's not fair that somebody just comes out of nowhere and goes straight to the door and maybe fills up the last seat."

While polling suggests pocketbook issues such as the price of gas and diesel are top of mind for midterm voters, those who back either Paxton or Talarico often bring up values as the chief motivator of their support.
Daniel Mitchell attended the Talarico rally in Fort Worth wearing a black T-shirt with the words "I'm a Talafreako," co-opting the derisive nickname that Trump and others have used for the Democrat.
"I think what [Talarico] is doing for Texas is great, how he presents an idea that we can have a change that uplifts everyone," Mitchell told CBC News.

Mitchell's view of the Republican candidate? "Paxton's a fraud," he said. "Just down to his personal life and the policies he's supporting, you can tell that he sells out for whatever makes him happiest in the moment."
After Paxton's rally in the Dallas suburb of Allen, supporters wrote messages on his campaign bus. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
Paxton's personal life came under public scrutiny last year when his wife, a Texas state senator, filed for divorce, citing "biblical grounds" and accusing him of adultery.
Neither that nor the corruption allegations sway the Christians who are among Paxton's most ardent backers.
At Paxton's rally in Allen, attendees wrote messages of support on the campaign bus, many on Christian themes.
Mardi Day, a resident of nearby Plano, chose "Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord" as her message.
"I believe that's how the United States is going to stay a strong nation, by following Jesus Christ and our Constitution," Day told CBC News.
Another rally attendee, Gloria Jones, said her top political priority is undoing what she called a "massive immigration problem" from Arab countries.
"How are we going to get rid of all these radical Muslims?" Jones said. "They want to practise Sharia, they need to go back to their country and practise there."

Steve Ceh is a pastor at Solomon's Porch Ministries in New Braunfels, Tex., and a member of Pastors for Paxton, a group of 27 Christian leaders who endorsed the Republican candidate. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Steve Ceh, pastor of Solomon's Porch Ministries in New Braunfels, a city of 120,000 near San Antonio, is one of 27 Pastors for Paxton, a statewide group of Christian leaders praying for the Republican candidate.

"Every man that runs and every woman that runs is a flawed person," Ceh said when asked by CBC News to describe Paxton's positive traits. "So we look beyond the personality of that person and we vote policy, and he is directly in line with Christian values."
Ceh criticizes Talarico for what he calls a "severe leftist ideology" that can't co-exist with biblical principles.
"In Texas, when you start to threaten people's beliefs, values, they're going to go out and vote," he said. "[Talarico] will not win in Texas. I'm not even worried about it."

Trump, however, is worried enough about it that he has travelled to four cities in Texas since Oct. 1 to urge the MAGA faithful to get behind Paxton and raising the spectre that Democrat control of Congress would mean "communists" in power.
"You have to vote for Ken," Trump told a rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday. "Otherwise, all of the great things we've done are going to change very quickly."

articles.title: France braces for 3rd weekend of discord as youth-led protests spread across Europe

paras.en: France braces for 3rd weekend of discord as youth-led protests spread across Europe
High school students began demonstrating against school conditions last month

France prepared Saturday for a third consecutive weekend of protests over living costs and education, deploying 70,000 police and gendarmes and rerouting the Paris march to the capital's edge as youth-led demonstrations spread across Europe.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween.

Paris police banned union and "yellow vest" marches through the city centre, ordering demonstrations to follow a single route along the capital's outer boulevards, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton. Unions and student groups challenged the restrictions in court but lost in a last-minute legal battle.
President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that marches would stay out of city centres to protect shops.
Police also barred entry to Place de la République and Les Halles, both hit by rioting and looting on Oct. 17, Saturday night into Sunday morning.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Élysées. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protesters scuffle with riot police during a demonstration against rising living costs, in Paris on Oct. 17. (Emma Da Silva/The Associated Press)
The movement began with high school students protesting school conditions and broadened into anger over living costs.

Authorities counted about 550,000 protesters nationwide on Oct. 17, when rioters looted hundreds of shops, and 410,000 last Saturday, when rallies were largely peaceful, but police made more than 1,300 arrests.

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — urged protests in some 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life" and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said more than 140,000 people had signed up online.
- Audio What's behind the youth protests in France?
- Tens of thousands march in France as protests continue over schools and living costs

Berlin police expected about 10,000 people at the Brandenburg Gate. Some shops on the Kurfürstendamm boulevard boarded up their windows, although authorities said they were unaware of specific threats of violence. Protests were expected to begin in the early afternoon.

In Barcelona, Catalan police planned to activate their highest-level alert after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings. Rioting in the Spanish city last Saturday led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.
Italian police were on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna, and calls to protest circulated on TikTok in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.

articles.title: Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine-held territory

paras.en: Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine-held territory
Their evacuation is part of a major rescue operation carried out under a six-day ceasefire
Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have crossed into Ukrainian-held territory after a humanitarian mission and localized ceasefire.

"As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. All of them will receive the assistance they need," said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, thanking the U.S. and Melania Trump for mediation.
Ukrainian officials greeted the evacuees with posters reading "You're not alone" and "We embrace with our hearts."

The residents travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. The crossing took place under restrictions imposed by Ukrainian authorities that did not permit the disclosure of the number of evacuees or the location of the border crossing.
Ukrainian organizers said the restrictions were imposed in part to safeguard residents who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect the safety of similar humanitarian missions that may occur.

It was a rare joint Russia-Ukraine humanitarian effort — a brief respite in the grim war. The ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region began at 3 a.m. local time Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.

Civilians from Oleshky, on the Dnipro River, began the long journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday. The estimated 2,000 remaining residents were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

A resident evacuated from from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky reacts while being flanked by his daughter and wife, who were waiting to welcome him, as he returns to Ukrainian-controlled territory, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, at an undisclosed location on Saturday. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)
Supply routes to Oleshky have been disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said those who chose to travel from Oleshky to Ukrainian-held territory were taken to the Russian city of Anapa and flown to the Belarusian city of Homel. They were accompanied by Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, it said.
Daughters wait to see their fathers again
Relatives waited on Saturday at the border between Ukraine and Belarus, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them.
Volunteers from organizations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father more than two years ago, was among those waiting. Paliy, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory at the time, while he stayed behind.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbours but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no [other] way, and he walked us to the road and that was it," Pavlyn said of the last time she saw her father.
- Video Russia, Ukraine team up on relief effort in Russian-occupied Oleshky
- Melania Trump, Pope Leo broker humanitarian ceasefire for ravaged Ukraine city Oleshky
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

Russia's ombudsperson and lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia. Russian media outlets on Saturday showed civilians arriving at a temporary accommodation site in Simferopol on the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Two evacuees wearing Ukrainian flags feed their cat after arriving at an undisclosed location on Ukrainian-controlled territory on Saturday. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

A video shared by Ukraine's ombudsman showed dozens of Oleshky residents slowly disembarking from a plane at a Belarusian airfield. Many people were elderly. Some required help to walk, and a few were carried on stretchers or in wheelchairs. They carried minimal luggage — only a bag or two. Dogs were unloaded from the plane in cages.

As several big buses crossed into Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region from Belarus, the residents were greeted by relatives. Ambulances lined the street and several large military tents were erected where hot meals, tea and medical aid were provided.

Animals were among those who made the journey on Saturday, with Ukrainian emergency services, Red Cross and UAnimals NGO employees handling the pets of residents evacuated from Oleshky into Ukrainian-held territory. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)
Pet food and water bottles were piled up on several tables.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
U.S. approves Patriot missile sales for Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday welcomed U.S. approval of Ukraine’s purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors but urged partners to supply the weapons from existing stocks to protect the country this winter, warning the newly authorized U.S. sale could take years to deliver.

"Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

The Trump administration said Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion US sale of Patriot air defence interceptors, after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of the vital munition needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles.
The U.S. State Department said 500 Patriot missiles would be purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.
A Ukrainian drone attack kills 2 in Russia

Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
- Russia, Ukraine begin ceasefire in city of Oleshky as deadly strikes continue elsewhere
- Melania Trump, Pope Leo broker humanitarian ceasefire for ravaged Ukraine city Oleshky
Russia's Ministry of Defence said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.
Zelenskyy urged partners to impose further sanctions on Russia and provide new support packages to Ukraine.
"The world sees Russia targeting civilian infrastructure every day. Everyone who does not want to see this Russian escalation spread further into Europe must help Ukraine," he said in an online post.

articles.title: Human trafficking victims stranded in Guinea-Bissau
